articles.title: How Paper-Based Friction Materials Power Modern Machinery

paras.en: How Paper-Based Friction Materials Power Modern Machinery

Have you ever wondered what enables everything from roaring construction machinery to agricultural machinery plowing the fields to industrial equipment shuttling through factories—the precise starting, smooth operation, and reliable braking they achieve?

The answer lies in a seemingly insignificant yet crucial core component: friction material. It acts as the "safety guard" and "power link" of machinery, ensuring every brake is safe and effective, and every power transmission is smooth and flawless.

Among the vast family of friction materials, wet friction materials are becoming the new favorite in modern machinery due to their exceptional reliability, safety, and exceptionally long lifespan. Among wet materials, paper-based friction materials stand out as a leading force thanks to their excellent overall performance, cost-effectiveness, and broad application prospects.
Today, let's delve deeper into the fascinating world of this "unsung hero"—paper-based friction materials.
What is Paper-Based Friction Material? — A Sponge-Like Power Core
Imagine a "sponge" with countless tiny pores—that's the most intuitive image of paper-based friction material.

It is a material with a reticular porous structure composed of three core components: reinforcing fibers, functional fillers, and a binder resin. This unique structure gives it extraordinary capabilities:
- Oil Storage Capacity: The porous structure acts like a miniature "oil depot," capable of storing large quantities of lubricant.

- Dynamic Lubrication: When the friction plate and mating plate engage and are subjected to pressure, the lubricant within the material is instantly squeezed onto the friction surface, forming a tough lubricant film, enabling smooth, gentle "wet" friction.
- Self-Recovery: When the friction plates separate, the material rebounds like memory foam, "absorbing" the lubricant back into the pores, ready for the next operation.

It is this dynamic cycle of "oil storage-oil squeezing-oil return" that allows paper-based friction materials to perform well in an oil bath environment, achieving a perfect combination of high durability and stable friction performance.
Exploring Core Performance: How Do Three Key Factors Affect It?

The performance of paper-based friction materials is not static. Like a top athlete, its performance is influenced by the "field," "equipment," and "condition." Let's examine how these three key factors shape its performance.
Factor 1: The "Stage Effect" of Lubricants

Paper-based friction materials are highly sensitive to lubricants, and different lubricants create distinct "stages" for their performance. Even the same friction material can exhibit significantly different friction characteristics (especially the kinetic friction coefficient) when exposed to different lubricants.
Figure 1: Kinetic friction coefficient curve for a paper-based friction material in gear oil
Figure 2: Dynamic friction coefficient curve of the same material in hydraulic oil

Interpretation: The above chart clearly shows that the same material behaves very differently in gear oil and hydraulic fluid. Furthermore, various additives added to lubricating oils (such as dispersants and anti-wear agents) can interact complexly with the material surface, further affecting its friction properties. Therefore, choosing the right oil for paper-based friction materials is the first step in achieving optimal performance.
Density is a trump card for paper-based friction materials. It is directly related to the material's porosity, leading to a delicate balancing act in terms of performance.

High density (low porosity) means a denser material, resulting in better strength and thermal conductivity, lower wear rate, and longer life. However, the downside is reduced oil storage capacity, which can lead to a lower coefficient of friction and compromise power transmission.

Low density (high porosity) means the material is more porous, resulting in greater oil storage capacity and a higher coefficient of friction, which can provide greater braking force or transmit torque. However, the downside is reduced mechanical strength and wear resistance, shortening service life.
Figure 3: Comparison of the dynamic coefficient of friction for materials of varying densities (Type 2 to Type 6, increasing density)
Figure 4: Comparison of wear rates of materials with different densities

Interpretation: Figures 3 and 4 vividly illustrate this balancing act. There's no such thing as absolute good or bad, only suitability. When selecting a paper-based friction material, the optimal trade-off between friction coefficient and durability must be determined based on specific application requirements (e.g., high torque versus long life).
Factor 3: Extreme Challenges of Operating Conditions

In addition to oil type and density, actual operating conditions, such as surface pressure, sliding speed, and oil temperature, pose extreme challenges to paper-based friction materials. These factors directly affect the temperature of the friction interface, the thickness and stability of the oil film, and thus dynamically alter the coefficient of friction.

Therefore, please remember: the coefficient of friction of a particular paper-based friction material is not a fixed value, but rather a performance range determined through extensive and repeated testing under specific operating conditions.
Broad Applications: Injecting a Powerful "Heart" into Machinery

Thanks to its excellent overall performance and customizability, Carlisle Brake & Friction's paper-based friction materials have been successfully applied to the core components of various heavy-duty machinery, becoming their powerful and reliable "heart."
We understand that different machines and applications require significantly different friction materials. For example:
- Service brakes for construction machinery (such as excavators and loaders) require materials that provide a stable, powerful braking force under high loads to ensure safety.
- Powershift transmissions for agricultural machinery (such as tractors) require materials that provide smooth engagement and excellent heat resistance to handle frequent shifting.
- Clutches for industrial machinery require materials that respond quickly and have a long lifespan to ensure continuous and efficient operation of production lines.

To this end, Carlisle Brake & Friction has developed a series of special paper-based friction materials for different application scenarios, providing each customer with the most suitable and reliable solution.
Continuous Innovation, Driving the Future
Technological advancement is endless. To meet increasingly demanding application requirements and broaden market prospects, Carlisle Brake & Friction remains at the forefront of innovation.

We are not only continuously optimizing the formulation and processing of paper-based friction materials to push their performance limits, but are also actively exploring next-generation wet friction materials with even higher performance. These R&D efforts have made significant progress, aiming to provide global customers with more diverse and advanced options, driving the infinite possibilities of future machinery.

articles.title: Celebrating 100-Years with Medina Mayor and Employees

paras.en: Celebrating 100-Years with Medina Mayor and Employees

MEDINA, OHIO — September 24, 2025 — Carlisle Brake & Friction (CBF), a global leader in the development and manufacture of high-performance brake and friction solutions, today welcomed Medina Mayor Dennis Hanwell, Economic Development Director Kimberly Marshall, and Executive Director of the Medina Chamber of Commerce Jaclyn Ringstmeier, for a special photo op at the company’s headquarters, located at 920 Lake Road. The event was a commemorative celebration of CarlisleCBF’s 100-year anniversary and its enduring presence in the Medina community.

paras.en: The photo op featured Mayor Hanwell alongside Carlisle’s Operations Leader, David Smith, and a number of employees who have been with the company for decades. The occasion honored CarlisleCBF’s century of innovation and its deep roots in the Medina area, where it has been a significant employer and community partner.

"We are incredibly proud of our history and our strong connection to the city of Medina," said David Smith. "This milestone is a testament to the hard work and dedication of our employees, many of whom have been with us for decades. We are grateful for the continued support of Mayor Hanwell and the entire Medina community."

The photo op followed a recent employee and family event at the Medina plant that celebrated the 100-year milestone. The celebration was filled with games, face painting, food, and fun for all ages, reinforcing the company's commitment to its employees and their families.

Mayor Hanwell expressed his gratitude for CarlisleCBF’s presence in the city. “Carlisle has been a part of the Medina community for nearly 65 years, providing good jobs and a strong economic foundation,” said Mayor Hanwell. "We are proud to celebrate their 100-year anniversary and recognize the significant role they have played in our city’s growth and prosperity."
CarlisleCBF, a brand of CentroMotion, was founded in 1925 and has grown to become a global leader in its field, serving a wide range of markets including agriculture, construction, and mining.

Carlisle Brake & Friction, a CentroMotion brand, is a leading global provider of highly engineered and integrated brake and friction solutions for a wide range of industrial applications. With over 100 years of experience, the company is dedicated to delivering innovative, reliable, and high-performance products to its customers worldwide.

articles.title: Bumper Removal & ADAS Recalibration
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Removing a front bumper cover for repairs or modifications can affect advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS). Cameras, radar and other sensors require precise alignment to function properly.

Remind customers that bumper removal or replacement may require ADAS recalibration, even during routine radiator, condenser or headlight repairs. Always consult manufacturer procedures to ensure proper operation and safety.

articles.title: BendPak Introduces OctaFlex Series Two-Post Lift
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: BendPak Inc. has introduced the OctaFlex Series, turning its eight-arm car lift concept into a production model. The two-post lift is designed to improve bay productivity, technician ergonomics and operational precision. The BendPak OctaFlex 12DPS two-post lift is now shipping.

Since introducing the OctaFlex concept in 2024, BendPak refined it based on customer feedback and lab testing. The OctaFlex 12DPS combines a traditional 12,000-lb. capacity two-post lift with an integrated 6,000-lb. capacity lift-assist system.

While the four primary arms support the vehicle, the four secondary arms can raise, lower or hold cabs, drivetrains, EV batteries, suspension assemblies and other heavy components without additional equipment, helpers or bays. When not required, the auxiliary arms can be moved up out of the way so the lift can be used as a standard two-post model.

Also unique to the patent-pending OctaFlex Series is a magnetic pendant controller with two-speed controls. The pendant lets technicians stand back from the lift columns for visibility around the vehicle. Each set of arms can be operated independently at either “normal” or “slow” speed.

“As dealers and independent repair shops continue to struggle with an aging and shrinking technician workforce, they also face surging demand for labor-intensive tasks like cab-off repairs and EV service,” said Jeff Kritzer, president and CEO of BendPak. “OctaFlex eases the pressure by helping technicians handle complex jobs independently with greater efficiency and less physical strain, maximizing throughput and profit potential.”
Dave’s Auto Center in Centerville, Utah, performs multiple cab-offs every day across its 25 bays. After installing an OctaFlex lift, owner Dave Bell says it saves hours in production.

“OctaFlex is a gamechanger if you’re pulling cabs off trucks,” said Bell. “Not only does it make the cab-off process easier, but since you can raise the chassis while the cab is in the air, you can do brake work, suspension work, change the oil — a lot of the extra jobs customers want done while their truck is in the shop — while you’re waiting for parts. It’s significantly more efficient than finishing the cab-off first and then completing the remaining work after the truck is back together.”

On average, shops can save two hours per cab-off operation using OctaFlex. If an OctaFlex bay is used to pull 20 cabs a month, a shop with a $150 hourly labor rate can generate an additional $6,000 in revenue every month, or $72,000 a year. Customers can calculate their return on investment at BendPak.com/OctaFlex.

Additional labor savings come from eliminating the need for a second technician or helper. OctaFlex can improve bay utilization and throughput by enabling all work to be completed in a single bay rather than tying up two bays for one vehicle.

Removing a cab often requires the tech to spend time on the floor checking that everything is disconnected. Because OctaFlex holds both the chassis and the cab, technicians can stand throughout the process. With everything at eye level, technicians can work with improved ergonomics. It also eliminates the need to manually move heavy vehicle components or lift tables.
As a result, technicians are safer, less fatigued and less likely to experience workplace injuries.

The OctaFlex 12DPS features BendPak’s Automatic Swing Arm Restraint System (ASARS) to keep the primary lift arms in place. ASARS provides a full 360-degree grip with 10 times the holding power to lock the lift arms in place under the vehicle.
OctaFlex has been third-party tested and ALI Certified (listed as model EV12DPS) to meet industry safety and performance standards.

Reuniting the body and chassis can be the most difficult part of a cab-off. OctaFlex keeps the chassis and cab aligned on the lift throughout the procedure so the technician can move them together using the pendant controller.
Visit BendPak.com/OctaFlex to learn more about the OctaFlex 12DPS, including specifications, photos, videos and an interactive ROI calculator.
The OctaFlex 12DPS will be featured at the SEMA Show Nov. 3-6 in Upper South Hall booth no. 36129.

articles.title: What to Know About Modern Windshield Replacement
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Butyl rubber was commonly used to install windshields decades ago but is unsuitable for modern vehicles. Today’s windshields use structural adhesives that help maintain vehicle integrity during collisions.

Counter pros should recommend manufacturer-approved windshield adhesives rather than butyl rubber. Proper installation is critical, especially on vehicles equipped with ADAS cameras that require calibration following windshield replacement.
This video is sponsored by The Pronto Network.

articles.title: Texas State Technical College hosts auto collision Battle Royale
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: Texas State Technical College (TSTC) Waco’s Auto Collision and Management program recently hosted its first Battle Royale competition at the Fentress Center.

Students competed in collision repair and refinishing contests, depending on the certificate or associate degree program they are pursuing, an Instagram post from the college states. The contests included dent repair, marking, panel blocking, and preparation. Students also completed an interview for the competition.
The provost’s office at the Waco campus provided scholarship funding for the winning students, and industry partners supported the event through sponsorships and in-kind donations, the post adds.
Local news station KWTX reports industry representatives attended the event to observe the competition and connect with prospective technicians.
Competitor Nery Martinez, a refinishing student, told KWTX the event introduced him to the high-pressure demands of the trade.

“Today, we got an interview, which is most important; we got to run down how an interview goes, and we got to mask a car, basically showing us if we can handle how to mask a car the right, proper way,” Martinez said in the newscast.
Martinez works prep with his father at Alliance Collision and told KWTX that automotive painting runs in his family.

“I want to give props to my Dad. He’s a painter himself to this day,” Martinez told the news station. “He graduated from this school about 20 years ago, and he motivates me every day just to keep pushing. Because he did it, why can’t I?”
TSTC provides hands-on training, Martinez told KWTX.

“It’s stressful, of course, but deep down, you’ve got to give it what you got. It’s not about the next person beside you,” Martinez said in the interview. “That’s how it is in the real world; they ask for what you got, not what your partner got.”
- Second place: Horacio Gonzalez of Hillsboro
- Third place: Osvaldo Agonizante of Waco
- First place: Jacob Parga of Fort Worth
- Second place: Leah Coleman of Wichita Falls
- Third place: Angel Becerril of Corsicana
Photos courtesy of Texas State Technical College

articles.title: Auto insurer switching up despite no change in YoY shopping
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: The Q3 Quarterly Insurance Signals Intelligence Report from JD Power and TransUnion shows auto insurance carrier switching increased even though year-over-year (YoY) shopping was flat.
The latest report shows shopping reached 13.2% and switching 5.1%, both up 0.6 percentage points from Q2.
“Looking at longer-term auto trends, shopping has flattened while switching has continued to increase; this could signal a potential for continued retention pressure on carriers,” the report states.
Among auto insurer switchers, the median premium amount moving carriers was more than $3,300 in Q3, according to the report.

According to the report’s Auto Loyalty Tracker, NJM, Erie, USAA, Country Financial, and Mercury had higher customer loyalty, while Nationwide, Alfa, Direct Auto, Root, and National General had lower loyalty.

“After a cool-down in shopping in Q2, shop rates rose again beginning in July and remained elevated through the end of Q3,” the report states. “Switching rose considerably, hitting a record high in August of 5.3% before falling slightly to 5.0%, equaling the prior record recorded in July.”
It adds that consumers are finding fewer opportunities for meaningful savings through switching carriers as rate actions moderate and premium increases stabilize.
“Auto shopping growth has slowed significantly from the elevated levels observed during 2024 and 2025, signaling a more normalized market environment,” the report states.
The report also highlights shopping and switching trends in home and renters insurance lines.
Lastly, it notes that AI agents like Meta Muse could drive shopping and switching higher by making it easier for consumers to find better rates.
Previous Quarterly Insurance Signals Intelligence reports are available here.
In a new whitepaper, LexisNexis Risk Solutions details survey findings on auto insurance shopping trends, stating that 72% of consumers who shopped for auto insurance are open to switching carriers.
Of the 72%, 17% said they were definitely seeking a new auto insurance company. Eighty-seven percent said the auto insurance shopping experience was easier than expected or met their expectations.

“Consumers are increasingly treating auto insurance as an ongoing value comparison, not a one-time renewal decision,” said Jeff Batiste, LexisNexis Risk Solutions auto and home senior vice president and general manager, in a press release. “Our research shows that many auto insurance shoppers are open to switching, but price and perceived value ultimately determine whether they stay or leave. For insurance carriers, auto shopping behavior can be an early signal of competitive pressure and retention risk, and the ability to identify and act on those signals sooner can help retain profitable policyholders while uncovering opportunities to acquire new customers.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: LexisNexis Risk Solutions says, according to its research:
- “Consumers are cost-conscious and willing to compare policy options, and many find the shopping experience easier than expected.
- “Price often outweighs loyalty in both switching and staying decisions.
- “While bundled policies still exhibit higher retention, bundling alone may not protect insurance carriers from consumers evaluating options.
- “Insurance affordability is becoming a key part of the vehicle purchase decision.
- “Auto and insurance-related events have a much greater impact on auto insurance shopping than life events.”

“When insurers raised rates broadly to restore profitability, they triggered a comparison-shopping habit that persists even as some rate decreases are taking effect today,” LexisNexis Risk Solutions says in the press release. “That focus on cost extends beyond the switching decision, with price continuing to outweigh loyalty even after consumers choose a new insurance carrier.”
According to recent LendingTree survey results, half of Americans with auto or home insurance have avoided filing a claim largely because they fear their premiums would go up.
Nearly three-quarters (73%) of “claim avoiders” said their most recent situation involved car insurance.

articles.title: AkzoNobel updates basecoat blending practices in technical bulletin
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: AkzoNobel has released an updated technical service bulletin that significantly expands on the area needed to perform an effective color blend.

“A lot of times we are challenged with helping customers have a way to explain or provide information to an insurer or a customer or anybody else about the blend operation and how much room it takes to blend,” Greg Askew, AkzoNobel North America technical services specialist, automotive and speciality coatings vehicle refinishes, told Repairer Driven News (RDN).
Ultimately, Askew said technicians consider multiple factors and use their judgment on each repair.

“We are laying out what those considerations and factors are that determine how much space it may take to blend a color and if it’s going to fall into an adjacent panel,” Askew said about the bulletin.

The bulletin says that the goal is to achieve an undetectable color blend while keeping the overall repair area as small as practical. It adds that maintaining the color blend within the repaired panel may be suitable and is the preferred method for economy and efficiency when sufficient space is available.
“However, when planning the area needed for blending, it is important to consider the completed repair rather than just the original dent or scratch,” the bulletin states.

Preparation includes a sanded feather-edge for a smooth transition through the existing coating layers into the OEM clearcoat. This transition extends a few inches beyond the original damage and becomes part of the area where primer surfacer is applied, according to the bulletin.

Sanding the applied primer surfacer also requires a smooth transition into the surrounding finish, the bulletin adds. This sanding extends a few inches beyond the primer surfacer application area and further increases the size of the completed repair.

Sealer may be applied over the sanded primer surfacer, depending on the specifics of the repair and the technician’s judgement, the bulletin notes. This would extend the repair area beyond the sanded edge of the primer surfacer.

“The area needed to achieve a seamless color blend is influenced by several factors,” the bulletin states. “These include the type and extent of damage, additional sanding and filling, color application characteristics, and the location and geometry of the panel. Style lines and changes in panel angle can influence how effectively the available area can be used for blending. Translucent colors may require a ground coat or additional basecoat application, while some colors or specific paint technology may require a wet bed. These factors should be considered when determining the overall space needed for the repair.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: According to the bulletin, the available blend area must also allow for the clearcoat application. At the edge of the blend panel, AkzoNobel recommends only one coat of clearcoat to limit a perceived color shift caused by differing clearcoat depth.

However, all applied basecoat, including any wet bed, requires two coats of clearcoat to provide the necessary UV protection for the basecoat binder and pigments, the bulletin states. Basecoat and wet bed must therefore remain within the area receiving the two coats of clearcoat.

AkzoNobel adds that a clearcoat-only area extending two to four inches inward from the blend-panel edge is a reasonable planning allowance. The technician’s judgment and application technique should determine the actual extent.

“Based on AkzoNobel technical team field experience and training practice, the following groups provide general guidance for planning the blend area across basecoat systems,” the bulletin states. “Blend distances are measured outward from the final repair area edge, including any extension resulting from sealer application. The distances are general planning guidelines rather than specific requirements. Detailed application methods remain subject to the applicable TDS and any color-specific instructions. “
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Askew said the document doesn’t cover every specific scenario but tries to encompass the most common repair considerations.
“We try to be as neutral as possible because all of it’s still a judgment and there’s so many variables,” Askew said.
The bulletin was expanded to assist repairers in communicating some of these variables, he said.

“Somebody that’s not familiar with the repair process and blending thinks, ‘Well, here’s the dent and so you’ve got plenty of room to blend,’” Askew said. “But once the dent is repaired, it grows. The damage to the paint is expanded. Once you fix that edge, that edge is extended even further. Then you have to apply primer, which extends the edge a little bit further. Then, when you sand that primar edge, it extends it a little bit further. Then if you put sealer on it, which is a choice, it is going to grow that edge even more.”

paras.en: AkzoNobel and Axalta Coating Systems also recently announced that the combined company will use the name Axanzo after their intended merger is complete.

“We’re excited to announce the new name for our combined company,” said Greg Poux-Guillaume, AkzoNobel CEO, in a news release. “Axanzo signals a bold new start for a company which will be stronger in every way. It’s a launchpad for going further and faster than we ever could alone, embodying the pace and power to innovate, the strength to deliver and the excellence to succeed.”
Poux-Guillaume will be the company’s new CEO.

Chris Villavarayan, CEO of Axalta, who will be deputy CEO of the combined company, adds: “Axanzo will continuously reset the standard of what coatings can do. The new name perfectly captures our shared ambition to push boundaries, honoring our heritage and offering an exciting glimpse of what’s to come.”
Both companies will continue to operate independently until closing, expected in early 2027.

articles.title: Alignment Specs: 2021–Current Ford Mustang Mach-E
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: The Mustang Mach-E uses Ford’s Global Electrified 1 (GE1) platform, a heavily reworked version of the automaker’s C2 architecture. The C2 platform also underpins the fourth-generation Ford Focus and third-generation Kuga, as well as the fourth-generation Escape. While the Mach-E shares its platform lineage with these vehicles, GE1 was adapted for an all-electric SUV. That platform connection provides useful context for technicians approaching its suspension and alignment service, while vehicle-specific procedures and specifications remain essential across model years and configurations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Mustang Mach-E has adjustable camber and toe at both ends, but an alignment service with this car also calls for attention to the vehicle loading, ride height and driver-assistance systems. The procedures provided in this article are for a 2023 AWD Mach-E, so confirm the specifications and service procedure for the vehicle’s exact model year and configuration before making adjustments. The supplied information does not include numerical alignment specifications or acceptable ride-height ranges.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Before measuring toe, Ford’s procedure calls for a level surface, correct tire pressure, and an inspection for tire wear, damage and suspension wear or damage. The steering wheel must be held straight ahead with a suitable holding device during the toe checks.

Ride-height measurement has additional preparation requirements. Position the vehicle on a flat, level surface with tires inflated to the correct pressure. The procedure specifies a full tank of fuel, proper fluid levels and no cargo in the cabin or bed. Inspect for aftermarket equipment and changes to steering, suspension, wheels or tires, then jounce the front and rear suspension vigorously to let the vehicle settle.

Remember: Alignment readings are only useful when the vehicle is in the specified condition. If ride height is incorrect, look for changes or problems in the suspension and review the vehicle’s service information before treating alignment adjustments as the solution.

If you find that you can’t get the vehicle to roll to carry out the rolling compensation measurements, this is because it has Rollaway Protection Mode that activates when the car is turned off and the driver exits. To enable the car to roll, you will have to leave it on and in neutral during the alignment. In some cases, you might want to attach the driver seatbelt and roll the door latch to prevent it from going into park.

Front camber is adjusted at the strut-to-knuckle connection. First, measure camber with alignment equipment, then remove the wheels and tires. The brake flexible hose is unbolted and moved aside, and the wheel knuckle is supported with mechanic’s wire.

The original strut-to-knuckle bolts and nuts are removed and discarded. Ford specifies new service bolts and nuts for reassembly. The service fasteners are smooth and smaller in diameter than the splined original equipment bolts. With the new fasteners installed and snug, move the knuckle inboard or outboard to bring camber into specification. The procedure states that moving from the maximum inboard to maximum outboard position provides 0.5 degree of adjustment.

Do not fully tighten the strut-to-knuckle fasteners until camber is corrected. After adjustment, torque the bolts and nuts to 173 lb.-ft. (235 Nm). Reinstall the brake hose and torque its bolt to 97 lb.-in. (11 Nm). Reinstall the wheels and tires, recheck alignment and adjust front toe if needed. Because changing camber can affect toe, finish by verifying the toe readings.

Front toe is adjusted at the inner tie rods. With the steering wheel held straight, check toe on both sides. Hold each outer tie-rod end stationary while loosening its jam nut; Ford cautions that allowing the tie-rod end to turn can damage the boot. Move the steering gear boot clamp aside, then rotate the inner tie rod to adjust toe. Do not let the steering gear bellows twist as the inner tie rod turns. Recheck toe after adjustment and road test the vehicle.

Rear camber is adjusted by moving the upper control arm at its inboard mounting point. Measure camber, loosen the inboard nut approximately two turns, then slide the control arm inboard or outboard to change the reading. Recheck the alignment to verify the change and adjust rear toe if needed. The supplied procedure lists a torque of 76 lb.-ft. (103 Nm) for the upper control arm inboard nut.

Rear toe is adjusted at the toe link. With the steering wheel held straight ahead, measure toe on both sides. Before turning the toe-link bolt, clean the area around the joint using mild liquids. Ford notes that the cam nut and cam bolt area must be free of foreign material for proper clamping. Loosen the toe-link nut approximately one turn, rotate the toe-link bolt to obtain the specified reading, and tighten without disturbing the setting. The procedure lists 66 lb.-ft. (90 Nm) for the toe-link nut.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If the Mach-E is equipped with Lane Departure Warning, Ford requires an IPMA camera alignment after rear toe adjustment. Connect a scan tool and follow its directions for the camera alignment procedure. Road test after the adjustment and required camera service.

The supplied ride-height procedure uses a surface gauge to measure from a flat, level surface to suspension reference points. At the front, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm forward bolt and to the center of the ball-joint pinch bolt. Subtract the lower-arm forward-bolt measurement from the ball-joint pinch-bolt measurement to calculate front ride height.

At the rear, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm-to-subframe bolt and to the center of the lower arm-to-wheel-knuckle bolt. For the rear, subtract the wheel-knuckle-bolt measurement from the subframe-bolt measurement.

The service information provided describes how to take these measurements but does not give target ride-height values. Use the correct model-year service information for the vehicle to determine whether the recorded measurements are within specification. Avoid substituting a visual estimate or a generic ride-height value.

The vehicle’s service information shows a headlamp level sensor at both the front and rear suspension. The front sensor is mounted at the left front suspension, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. The rear sensor is also mounted at the left side, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. Each has an electrical connector.

During a suspension or alignment inspection, check that the sensors, brackets, arms and wiring are present and undamaged. The supplied procedure covers sensor removal and installation, but it does not specify an adjustment or calibration following a wheel alignment. If a sensor or its linkage has been disturbed or damaged, consult the correct service information for the required repair steps.

articles.title: PRI 2026 Education Program Promises Expert Insights
articles.author: Greg Jones

paras.en: Performance Racing Industry (PRI) will offer a range of educational opportunities at the 2026 PRI Show, Dec. 10-12, at the Indiana Convention Center and Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. The program will cover business strategies, motorsports engineering and career development, with sessions designed for professionals at different stages of their careers.
Friday, Dec. 11, will feature PRI Education sessions addressing key business and technical challenges facing motorsports, including:

- Using Tribology to Find Extra Horsepower (9 a.m.): Peter Lee of Southwest Research Institute and Lake Speed Jr. of SPEEDiagnostix will explain how reducing friction can improve engine and drivetrain performance.
- State of the Racing Market (11 a.m.): PRI Director of Market Research Gavin Knapp will discuss new research on industry performance, market conditions and business expectations.
- How a Culture Can Cure Your Crew Needs (1 p.m.): Tom Shay of Profits Plus Solutions will share strategies for attracting employees, improving retention and building a stronger workplace culture.

articles.title: Automotive Parts Headquarters Raises $513K for WACOSA
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Automotive Parts Headquarters Inc. (APH), together with its supplier partners and the Bartlett family, raised $513,000 through its annual fundraiser benefiting WACOSA, a central Minnesota nonprofit serving adults with disabilities. The 2026 event brings the fundraiser’s 14-year total to $3.7 million.
Proceeds support WACOSA programs that provide meaningful employment, day services and opportunities for more than 650 adults with disabilities across central Minnesota.

The event began with a walleye shore lunch and guided tours of WACOSA before attendees gathered at APH’s newest facility (a bulk storage warehouse) in St. Cloud for a pie and ice cream social celebrating its grand opening and APH’s “Building Our Future Together” initiative.

Attendees also participated in a hands-on art experience led by WACOSA artist-in-residence Dan Mondloch. The individual pieces created during the event will be incorporated into a collaborative collage inspired by the northern lights above a Minnesota lake.

“The day captured so much of what makes this event special,” said Jason Vogel, president of APH Stores Inc. “Bringing our supplier partners, employees and friends together to experience WACOSA’s mission firsthand, celebrate a new chapter for APH and create something together was incredibly rewarding.”

The day concluded with a cocktail reception, lobster-themed dinner and awards ceremony hosted by John and Nancy Bartlett at their home. A highlight of the evening was the presentation of a $513,000 check to Nancy Betts, executive director of WACOSA.

“Fourteen years of support from APH, its supplier partners and the Bartlett family has created a remarkable legacy for the people we serve,” Betts said. “This generosity creates opportunities for people to discover their strengths, contribute to their communities and pursue greater independence. We are deeply grateful for the lasting difference this partnership makes.”
Corey Bartlett, CEO and owner of APH, said the event reflects the generosity and commitment of the automotive aftermarket community.

“Every year, this event reminds us of the extraordinary generosity within the automotive aftermarket,” Bartlett said. “What began as a fundraiser has grown into a lasting partnership between APH, our supplier community and WACOSA. Seeing everyone come together to support the people and mission at the heart of WACOSA is what makes this event so meaningful.”
To view highlights from this year’s event, including the celebration, collaborative art project and messages from industry leaders, visit https://vimeo.com/autopartshq/wacosa26.

articles.title: Audi Matrix LED Headlights
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: LED headlights are changing the role of forward illumination. Before LEDs, forward lighting was just a bulb that cast its light in a pattern defined by the housing. Most of the innovation came with incandescent, halogen and Xenon bulbs. But light-emitting diodes (LEDs) are really a game changer for designers, engineers and technicians.

LED lights offer increased functionality by being able to control the brightness and pattern almost instantaneously. This is the case with Audi’s Matrix LED headlights found on the A8 and some E-Tron models. With these headlights, just the high-beam unit itself is made up of 25 individual segments. The small light-emitting diodes, which work in conjunction with lenses and reflectors connected in series, are activated and deactivated or dimmed individually according to the situation. This enables the system to react precisely to other cars, which it recognizes using a camera, and always illuminates the road brightly. Additional features of the new headlights are the intelligent cornering light, new-look daytime running lights and dynamic turn signals. The Audi Matrix LED headlights get the information they need from a camera, the navigation system and other sensors.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Composed of 1.3 million micromirrors per headlight, the units operate like movie projectors, emitting tiny unique particles or adaptable light. This is done with electrostatically controlled micromirrors that can adjust light beam pixels up to 5,000 times per second.

This lighting technology offers a selection of five different welcome/leaving animations when the vehicle is parked, each with unique motion graphics and text selected through the vehicle’s touchscreen display.

Audi’s lighting technology provides drivers with a 50-meter “light carpet” that is designed to keep light within the driver’s lane and extends the carpet left or right when changing lanes, and helps to avoid a “blinding” effect for oncoming traffic. Low-beam curved lighting bends below oncoming traffic, helping to illuminate people or objects on the side of the road that are otherwise difficult to detect. And on-ground light arrows help place the vehicle’s tires within its lane.

Early versions from 2020 in the U.S. lacked functions of the light carpet due to antiquated headlight laws that forbid adaptive lighting. Previously, the system could only show logos during startup and shutdown. On recent models, most of the European functionality has been enabled due to changes in headlight laws and adaptive lighting.

The good news is that the LED segments and lighting elements are expected to last the lifetime of the vehicle. But the units are sealed, and individual components inside can’t be serviced. The complete headlight assembly may cost in excess of $6,000 to replace.

The units are deeply integrated with the ADAS systems of the vehicle, including the Pre-Sense systems for automatic emergency braking. Having a scan tool that can talk to the ADAS system’s modules is critical. The ability to program replacement is also vital. Audi has issued several updates over the air and in new calibrations from the service information website.
The headlights are aimed and calibrated using a dynamic self-learning procedure that uses the forward-facing camera. If the camera is out of calibration, the headlights might not be aimed properly.

articles.title: Timing BMW VANOS N53 And N54
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: The BMW N53 (naturally aspirated) and N54 (turbocharged) engines were among the first BMW engines to come with variable valve timing on the intake and exhaust camshafts. The N53 and N54 straight-six have unfairly earned a bad reputation for reliability with technicians due to timing chain and variable valve timing problems. The reputation comes from owners not keeping up with oil changes and it is difficult to check engine timing.

The latest versions continuously adjust the position of the intake and exhaust camshafts for better power, efficiency and idle performance. The keyword to remember for a late-model VANOS system is that it works “continuously,” and not just under specific RPM ranges.

To service them, you will need the appropriate toolset to lock the crank and camshaft. You will also need a scan tool and scope to observe the crankshaft and camshaft signals to accomplish more advanced diagnostics.

Some newer systems can change the camshaft timing by as much as ±72 degrees. Dual-VANOS systems operate at all engine speeds. At lower engine speeds, the VANOS system opens the valves later during the intake stroke, increasing the vacuum and scavenging effect generated by the piston traveling downward in the cylinder. This improves idle quality and smooth power tip-in from a stop. As the engine rpm increases, the valves are opened earlier, enhancing torque as rpm increases. At higher engine speeds, the valves open later for full power delivery so the scavenging effect of the exhaust leaving the cylinder can pull more air into the cylinder. Hot rodders call this “valve overlap.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The system can augment and even eliminate the EGR valve by allowing some of the exhaust gas to remain in the combustion chamber to control combustion temperatures and NOX emissions.

Also, the camshaft position is changed to reduce engine warm-up times by allowing some unburned fuel to reach the catalytic converters. When the VANOS system on the N53 and N54 is not working, the most common symptoms are poor idle quality, reduced power and poor fuel economy. These symptoms are common to any other variable valve timing system, as well.
Like many variable valve timing systems, VANOS uses oil pressure-powered actuators to move the camshafts. The actuators need a consistent supply of oil for the correct viscosity, pressure and volume.
The N53 and N54 use a conventional cam phaser with internal chambers that hold pressurized oil that changes the position of the camshaft.
BMW N53 and N54 use an oil control valve like a lot of other variable valve timing engines. The solenoid is actuated by a pulse-width modulated signal.

If the oil is contaminated or is the wrong viscosity, the system can become sluggish. If the oil pressure can’t move the camshafts to the target positions in a specified time, the camshaft position sensors will sense it and set a code.

When oil pressure is not present, the camshafts go to a fully retarded position and are locked in place by a pin. A code will be set if the actuator and camshaft do not return to the correct position, because they are hydraulically jammed due to oil pressure leaking past a seal.

Disconnect the oil control valve if you are trying to scope a crankshaft and camshaft waveform. If this is not done, the waveform might look like the timing is out of sync because the engine will be adjusting the camshafts.
What Goes Wrong With N53 And N54 VANOS Systems?

The two most common failures for a VANOS system are related to the quality of the oil. The most common failure is when the O-ring seal on the piston wears out and allows oil pressure to move between the two chambers. This causes the actuator to be stuck or hydraulically jammed in either the full advance or retard positions.
When this happens, the actuator can’t fight the pressure exerted on the camshaft by the valve springs. This can cause a rattling noise at startup and idle.

If the oil is the wrong viscosity, it can cause the corrections to either retard or advance – in other words, to lag or happen too quickly. These changes take place in milliseconds. Depending on your scan tool and whether you can pull BMW DME or OBDII codes, the description may include the words jammed, stiff or lagging.

The engine will factor in the oil and coolant temperature into the time allowed for the actuation. If you have any codes related to these sensors, you might want to resolve these issues before troubleshooting the VANOS system.

Remind your customers that the quality of the oil in both engines matters to the life of their timing chains. BMW recommends a high-quality 5W-30 or 5W-40 that is fully synthetic and meets the BMW Longlife-01 FE specifications. These oils are formulated around the extended oil change interval. When a low-quality oil is used, it can break down before the oil change interval and accelerate wear on the links and pins of the timing chain.

articles.title: Wheel Speed Sensor Code? Test the Circuit Before Replacing the Hub
articles.author: Brake and Front End Staff

paras.en: An ABS warning light is on, and the scan tool shows a wheel speed sensor code. On many late-model vehicles, the sensor is part of the hub bearing assembly. That can make replacing the hub seem like the fastest solution.
But a wheel speed sensor code does not automatically condemn the sensor, bearing or hub assembly; it identifies a circuit or signal that needs to be tested.
Before replacing an expensive hub unit, confirm the integrity of the sensor, wiring and ABS module supply circuit.

Begin by verifying the complaint. Record all ABS, stability-control, communication and low-voltage codes before clearing anything. Check the code description and failure subtype in current service information. A circuit-open code, an implausible-signal code and an erratic-signal code can require different diagnostic approaches.
Next, monitor all four wheel-speed data parameters while rotating the wheels or driving the vehicle at low speed.
Compare the readings. Does one wheel remain at zero? Does its speed drop out intermittently? Does it report a different speed than the other three wheels?

This confirms which corner is producing the questionable data, but it still does not prove the hub is defective. The problem could be the sensor, magnetic encoder, connector, wiring harness, module supply voltage or even the vehicle’s electrical system.
The next step is to test the signal as close to the sensor as possible.

articles.title: Alignment Specs: 2021–Current Ford Mustang Mach-E
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: The Mustang Mach-E uses Ford’s Global Electrified 1 (GE1) platform, a heavily reworked version of the automaker’s C2 architecture. The C2 platform also underpins the fourth-generation Ford Focus and third-generation Kuga, as well as the fourth-generation Escape. While the Mach-E shares its platform lineage with these vehicles, GE1 was adapted for an all-electric SUV. That platform connection provides useful context for technicians approaching its suspension and alignment service, while vehicle-specific procedures and specifications remain essential across model years and configurations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Mustang Mach-E has adjustable camber and toe at both ends, but an alignment service with this car also calls for attention to the vehicle loading, ride height and driver-assistance systems. The procedures provided in this article are for a 2023 AWD Mach-E, so confirm the specifications and service procedure for the vehicle’s exact model year and configuration before making adjustments. The supplied information does not include numerical alignment specifications or acceptable ride-height ranges.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Before measuring toe, Ford’s procedure calls for a level surface, correct tire pressure, and an inspection for tire wear, damage and suspension wear or damage. The steering wheel must be held straight ahead with a suitable holding device during the toe checks.

Ride-height measurement has additional preparation requirements. Position the vehicle on a flat, level surface with tires inflated to the correct pressure. The procedure specifies a full tank of fuel, proper fluid levels and no cargo in the cabin or bed. Inspect for aftermarket equipment and changes to steering, suspension, wheels or tires, then jounce the front and rear suspension vigorously to let the vehicle settle.

Remember: Alignment readings are only useful when the vehicle is in the specified condition. If ride height is incorrect, look for changes or problems in the suspension and review the vehicle’s service information before treating alignment adjustments as the solution.

If you find that you can’t get the vehicle to roll to carry out the rolling compensation measurements, this is because it has Rollaway Protection Mode that activates when the car is turned off and the driver exits. To enable the car to roll, you will have to leave it on and in neutral during the alignment. In some cases, you might want to attach the driver seatbelt and roll the door latch to prevent it from going into park.

Front camber is adjusted at the strut-to-knuckle connection. First, measure camber with alignment equipment, then remove the wheels and tires. The brake flexible hose is unbolted and moved aside, and the wheel knuckle is supported with mechanic’s wire.

The original strut-to-knuckle bolts and nuts are removed and discarded. Ford specifies new service bolts and nuts for reassembly. The service fasteners are smooth and smaller in diameter than the splined original equipment bolts. With the new fasteners installed and snug, move the knuckle inboard or outboard to bring camber into specification. The procedure states that moving from the maximum inboard to maximum outboard position provides 0.5 degree of adjustment.

Do not fully tighten the strut-to-knuckle fasteners until camber is corrected. After adjustment, torque the bolts and nuts to 173 lb.-ft. (235 Nm). Reinstall the brake hose and torque its bolt to 97 lb.-in. (11 Nm). Reinstall the wheels and tires, recheck alignment and adjust front toe if needed. Because changing camber can affect toe, finish by verifying the toe readings.

Front toe is adjusted at the inner tie rods. With the steering wheel held straight, check toe on both sides. Hold each outer tie-rod end stationary while loosening its jam nut; Ford cautions that allowing the tie-rod end to turn can damage the boot. Move the steering gear boot clamp aside, then rotate the inner tie rod to adjust toe. Do not let the steering gear bellows twist as the inner tie rod turns. Recheck toe after adjustment and road test the vehicle.

Rear camber is adjusted by moving the upper control arm at its inboard mounting point. Measure camber, loosen the inboard nut approximately two turns, then slide the control arm inboard or outboard to change the reading. Recheck the alignment to verify the change and adjust rear toe if needed. The OEM procedure lists a torque of 76 lb.-ft. (103 Nm) for the upper control arm inboard nut.

Rear toe is adjusted at the toe link. With the steering wheel held straight ahead, measure toe on both sides. Before turning the toe-link bolt, clean the area around the joint using mild liquids. Ford notes that the cam nut and cam bolt area must be free of foreign material for proper clamping. Loosen the toe-link nut approximately one turn, rotate the toe-link bolt to obtain the specified reading, and tighten without disturbing the setting. The procedure lists 66 lb.-ft. (90 Nm) for the toe-link nut.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If the Mach-E is equipped with Lane Departure Warning, Ford requires an IPMA camera alignment after rear toe adjustment. Connect a scan tool and follow its directions for the camera alignment procedure. Road test after the adjustment and required camera service.

The ride-height procedure uses a surface gauge to measure from a flat, level surface to suspension reference points. At the front, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm forward bolt and to the center of the ball-joint pinch bolt. Subtract the lower-arm forward-bolt measurement from the ball-joint pinch-bolt measurement to calculate front ride height.

At the rear, measure from the surface to the center of the lower arm-to-subframe bolt and to the center of the lower arm-to-wheel-knuckle bolt. For the rear, subtract the wheel-knuckle-bolt measurement from the subframe-bolt measurement.

The service information provided describes how to take these measurements but does not give target ride-height values. Use the correct model-year service information for the vehicle to determine whether the recorded measurements are within specification. Avoid substituting a visual estimate or a generic ride-height value.

The vehicle’s service information shows a headlamp level sensor at both the front and rear suspension. The front sensor is mounted at the left front suspension, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. The rear sensor is also mounted at the left side, with its arm bracket attached to the lower arm. Each has an electrical connector.

During a suspension or alignment inspection, check that the sensors, brackets, arms and wiring are present and undamaged. The service procedure covers sensor removal and installation, but it does not specify an adjustment or calibration following a wheel alignment. If a sensor or its linkage has been disturbed or damaged, consult the correct service information for the required repair steps.

articles.title: REACH Acquires Carter and Airtex/ASC Brands
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: REACH announced the acquisition of the Carter Engineered Quality and Airtex/ASC brands, strengthening its water pump offering and expanding its product lineup to include fuel delivery components.

“We are proud to bring two iconic automotive aftermarket brands, Carter and Airtex/ASC, into a new era under the REACH umbrella,” said Dee Chen, CEO of REACH’s Global Automotive Business Unit. “By combining their rich heritage and trusted reputation with REACH’s global manufacturing strength, innovation and distribution network, we are committed to restoring their leadership and delivering exceptional value to customers worldwide.”
Under REACH ownership, Carter, Airtex and ASC will retain their individual brand identities. The company plans to expand part number coverage, increase inventory and relaunch each brand’s website.

REACH also outlined plans to expand the brands’ product offerings. Carter is expected to add fuel system components beyond its existing pump lineup. Airtex will continue offering cooling and fuel delivery products while expanding into engine components, including sensors. ASC will maintain its focus on heavy-duty water pump applications.
Carter and Airtex/ASC Bring Established Aftermarket History
Carter traces its history to 1909 and has manufactured automotive fuel delivery components for more than a century. Its product portfolio has evolved from carburetors to fuel pumps and water pumps.
Airtex, established in 1935, offers fuel delivery, cooling and electrical components. ASC, founded in 1976, specializes in water pumps, including heavy-duty applications for diesel engines.
The acquisition adds established aftermarket brands to REACH’s portfolio and supports its expansion into additional automotive replacement parts categories.

articles.title: V2X Market to Reach $4.05 Billion by 2035
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The V2X market is projected to grow from $0.50 billion in 2026 to $4.05 billion by 2035, at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 26.1% during the forecast period, according to MarketsandMarkets.

V2X adoption is driven by regulatory support for connected road safety, OEM integration of communication hardware, and the technical advantages of direct vehicle communication. C‑V2X uses LTE-based PC5 sidelink to exchange safety messages without relying on cellular network coverage, supporting low-latency V2V and V2I communication. Its ability to support non-line-of-sight communication, including around obstructing vehicles and buildings, improves awareness of hazards beyond the driver’s view, according to the MarketsandMarkets report.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While 4G cellular connectivity suffices for many network-based services, direct PC5 communication suits time-critical local safety messages, and 5G NR V2X supports more advanced use cases such as cooperative perception and coordinated driving. Regulatory action is reinforcing this shift, with the U.S. FCC adopting rules in November 2024 to transition ITS operations in the 5.9 GHz band toward C‑V2X. OEM adoption will depend on deployment scale, spectrum harmonization, interoperability, and availability of compatible roadside infrastructure.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: V2X deployment is expected to progress from connected-vehicle services already supported by cellular networks toward broader adoption of direct vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), and vehicle-to-pedestrian (V2P) communications. Priorities include collision avoidance, hazard alerts, and enhanced ADAS.

Over the next 2-3 years, Europe is expected to emerge as an early market for mass deployment of 5G‑V2X Direct–enabled vehicles and services, with 2026-2029 identified as a key rollout window. Beyond 2029, deployment is likely to expand toward vulnerable-road-user protection, infrastructure-enabled safety, and connected and automated driving.

In parallel, bidirectional V2X—particularly vehicle-to-home/building (V2H/V2B) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G)—could gain traction as smart charging, interoperability, and energy-market frameworks mature. This would enable EVs to support grid flexibility and renewable-energy integration.

V2V + V2N communication is gaining traction as C‑V2X platforms combine direct PC5 sidelink messaging for low-latency vehicle alerts with cellular Uu connectivity for cloud-based hazard notifications and traffic data. This configuration supports collision warnings, emergency braking alerts, and vehicle-generated hazard broadcasts alongside network-delivered road event information.

For instance, HARMAN introduced its Ready Aware V2N solution with HERE Technologies, enabling near-real-time alerts for sudden braking, stationary vehicles, road hazards, and intersection risks through 4G and 5G connectivity, including deployment through software updates in compatible connected vehicles. This development highlights opportunities for integrated V2V and V2N platforms, cellular telematics modules, and connected safety software across passenger cars and commercial vehicles, particularly in markets expanding connected mobility services.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Passenger Car Adoption and Platform Integration

Passenger cars are expected to support growing V2X demand as automakers incorporate vehicle connectivity into centralized electronic architectures and connected infotainment platforms. Integration of V2X with ADAS domain controllers enables external traffic signal data, approaching vehicle alerts, and road hazard messages to complement camera and radar inputs, particularly at blind intersections and in non-line-of-sight scenarios.

China’s vehicle-road-cloud integration pilot is advancing C‑V2X deployment, while European and Japanese OEMs are developing connected safety functions. For instance, the Honda Legend introduced Level 3 automated driving with cooperative safety technologies, while the Volkswagen Golf supports Car2X communication in equipped versions. These developments create opportunities for automotive-grade V2X chipsets, integrated telematics units, secure message processing, and standardized interfaces across vehicle platforms.

articles.title: ATA Names Mark Colson as Next President and CEO
articles.author: Kevin Linger

paras.en: The American Trucking Associations named Mark Colson as its next president and CEO, effective Dec. 1, 2026.

Colson currently serves as president and CEO of the Alabama Trucking Association, a role he has held since 2019. He brings more than two decades of experience in trucking advocacy, government affairs, and association leadership.

“This is a unique moment for ATA to make a renewed commitment to the trucking industry and the professionals who call our industry home,” Colson said. “It’s a commitment built first on earned trust, a sense of family and purpose, and an unrelenting passion to fight for the issues that matter most to trucking.”
Colson Brings State Association Experience

Before joining the Alabama Trucking Association, Colson held leadership roles at the Business Council of Alabama, including interim president, senior vice president of governmental affairs, and chief of staff.

His work within the ATA Federation includes service on ATA’s Strategic Priorities Committee and Truck PAC Board of Directors, along with the American Transportation Research Institute’s Research Advisory Committee.
In July 2026, Colson was elected vice chairman of the Trucking Association Executives Council, which represents executives from ATA-affiliated state associations and conferences.

“Few trucking companies operate within the borders of just one state, which is why the ATA Federation matters so much,” said Chris Maxwell, chairman of TAEC and president and CEO of the Rhode Island Trucking Association.
Read the full article on fleetequipmentmag.com.

articles.title: Counter Culture: Simplifying Belt Drive Repairs
articles.author: Counterman Staff

paras.en: In the latest episode of Counter Culture, Scott Howat, director of sales and marketing at Litens Aftermarket, discusses how the company applies its original equipment engineering expertise to develop automotive components that simplify installation and repairs.
Howat explains how Litens’ history of innovation, dating back to the first light tensioner installed on a 1979 Mustang, continues to influence its aftermarket products.
Litens Innovations Simplify Tensioner Installation
One example is the company’s patented Easy Button latch, which eliminates the need to remove and reinsert a tensioner pin during installation.
“Well, what happens if the pin just stayed on the tensioner?” Howat recalls an engineer asking during development.
Howat also highlights Litens’ Tech Assist Pin and lift features, which help technicians work in tight engine compartments and simplify tensioner replacement.
For counter professionals, Howat emphasizes the importance of considering the entire belt drive system when recommending replacement parts.
“A belt drive system was designed to perform together. It’s also designed to fail together,” he says.
Water Pump Kits Make Installation Easier

The conversation also explores Litens’ introduction of Dolz water pumps and Easy Fit kits to North America. These kits feature preattached gaskets and, on certain applications, pre-staked bolts to simplify installation.
Throughout the episode, Howat reinforces Litens’ focus on technician-friendly solutions, from complete accessory drive kits to installation hardware.
“We’re really taking this easy theme across all of our products,” Howat says, emphasizing the company’s commitment to making repairs easier for professional technicians.

articles.title: Parking Brake Sales: Looking Beyond the Cable
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: A parking brake cable may be the part the technician calls for, but it may not be the only part the job needs. A few targeted questions at the counter can uncover related components, service requirements and wear items. That will give counter pros the opportunity to build a more complete order and help the shop finish the repair with one delivery.

When diagnosing parking brake issues, the technician may need to inspect cables and related parts for wear, rust and corrosion; clean, replace or lubricate components; adjust the assembly; and verify operation. Electronic parking brakes add caliper-piston retraction and integrated-caliper adjustment requirements.

When a tech asks for a parking brake cable, first ask: What’s the vehicle, and is the concern a broken cable, excessive travel, inadequate holding or a parking brake that won’t release? Ask whether the technician has inspected the associated hardware for corrosion, wear,or binding. If it’s an integrated parking brake, ask whether the caliper requires a specific retraction or adjustment procedure. For electronic systems, ask whether there are indicator-light or wiring concerns.

Use those answers to build a complete order. If cables or mechanical components are being replaced, ask whether the technician has inspected the remaining parking-brake components and whether cleaning or lubrication is required. On drum-type applications, ask whether the shoes, springs, pins, self-adjusters, levers, clips, and related hardware have been inspected.

On disc applications, related caliper components and attaching hardware may also require inspection or replacement. And always remind the technician that adjustment and electronic caliper procedures must follow manufacturer recommendations.

articles.title: Study reveals new clues to why colorectal cancer in young people is so deadly
articles.author: Stephanie Pappas

paras.en: Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why.

A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients.

The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital.
"I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers."

Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations. It's now the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. for people under 50, and its numbers are even on the rise among children and adolescents.
Beyond questions about what's driving this uptick in cases, another mystery has been why this disease is so deadly in young people.
"The clinical data suggests that the disease in the younger patients is more aggressive overall," Anderson said. "The patients, being very healthy otherwise, do not do well with treatment."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To investigate that mystery, Anderson collaborated with Dr. Kimmie Ng, an oncologist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Dr. Ramnik Xavier, a gastroenterologist at the Broad Institute and Mass General Brigham. They used a method of analyzing RNA in cells that allowed them to work with frozen and banked tumor tissue. RNA, a cousin of DNA, reflects the genes that are active in cells. In all, the team analyzed 189 tumors: 54 from patients under 50 and 135 from patients over 50.

With that many samples, the researchers could look at gradual differences tied to each age group, instead of just comparing tumors between the younger and older groups overall. That enabled them to pinpoint subtle differences, Anderson said.

For starters, younger people had a higher proportion of connective tissue cells in their tumors than they did of malignant cancer cells. That pattern was flipped in patients of older ages. Having a smaller proportion of malignant cells might sound good, but connective tissue in tumors can secrete compounds that suppress the immune system, Anderson said. That helps protect the tumor from immune cells that might otherwise target its cells for destruction.

These connective tissue cells can also physically block chemotherapy drugs from getting to the cancerous cells. This could be one reason younger patients' cancers resist treatment, the researchers suggested.

Based on patterns of gene activity in the tumors, the researchers suspect that younger patients' cancer cells also show distinct activity related to cell-to-cell communication. That may help the cells migrate through the body more easily than cancer cells in older patients do. In other cancers, this kind of gene activity has been linked to more aggressive tumors and a greater chance that the disease will spread, or metastasize, Anderson said.

The study's results also turned up an intriguing mystery: the presence of lots of long noncoding RNA. These strands of RNA contain more than 200 building blocks, called nucleotides, that don't provide instructions for building proteins. Coding RNA, in contrast, is ferried to protein-building factories in cells to be used as blueprints.
Scientists don't know what much of this long noncoding RNA does in the body, nor do they understand what it is doing in the tumors specifically. However, they hope to find out.

Anderson and her team are already working on manipulating the RNA they found inside cancer cells in petri dishes. In time, this line of research could supply another piece of the puzzle, helping scientists understand why colorectal cancer is so aggressive in young people.
"It's a new avenue for research into this disease that we previously had no idea about," Anderson said.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice

Porter, C.B.M., et al. (2026) Insights into early-onset colorectal cancer from a single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of colorectal cancer across the age continuum. Nature Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04721-y

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: New simulation shows the first 2 billion years of the universe's history play out in stunning detail
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

paras.en: Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.
The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469

Elizabeth Howell was staff reporter at Space.com between 2022 and 2024 and a regular contributor to Live Science and Space.com between 2012 and 2022. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, speaking several times with the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.
