articles.title: Intrepid and Kinetic program will give premium discounts for ADAS procedures performed
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: A new program launched by Intrepid Direct and Kinetic ID could reduce business insurance costs for collision repair shops that recognize and complete ADAS procedures.

Nikhil Naikal, CEO and co-founder of Kinetic, told Repairer Driven News that the software is used by shops and insurance carriers to identify ADAS requirements when vehicles have been in a collision or if they had a mechanical repair done.

“Sensors on the vehicles can be disrupted or dislodged during the process of a repair and the requirements of calibrations are not very easy to know or understand,” Naikal said. “It is a hidden digital damage. Kinetic ID is a software that helps identify when reprogramming and calibrations are required.”
Intrepid Direct, which provides business insurance to collision repair facilities, have identified that the completion of proper ADAS procedures serves as a liability risk control, Naikal said.

“Collision repair keeps getting more complex, and shops are being asked to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated vehicle systems,” Bill Strout, president of Intrepid Direct, says in a press release. “This program gives our customers an easy way to build systematic ADAS review into their estimating and repair workflows through Kinetic ID Premium. Just as important, it creates a way to recognize shops that consistently identify and complete the right ADAS procedures, because those practices help reduce repair risk.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Through the use of Kinetic ID software, collision shops can qualify for additional liability and umbrella premium discounts, Naikal said. He adds that Intrepid Direct sees more use of the software and performance of ADAS calibrations as risk reducing behavior by the collision repair business.

“Their completed operations exposure goes down, and umbrella claims can go down,” Naikal adds. “Intrepid is recognizing that positive behavior and willing to reward that behavior with additional discounts.”
Identifying calibrations is important for vehicle repair, Naikal added.

“These sensors on the cars are no longer just convenience features,” he says. “They’re safety features. A vehicle that’s driving down the freeway at 60 miles per hour with a miscalibrated lane-keeping or lane-assist sensor behind the windshield or a blind spot monitoring system that doesn’t alert oncoming traffic in an adjacent lane can cause an accident and can be life-threatening for both the driver and passengers as well as the other vehicle.”
Failing to calibrate sensors can leave a vehicle not returned to its original state of safety, Naikal adds.
Naikal notes that Kinetic is a starting point that repair shops should use.

“The repairer is the one who has to make these decisions, and it could be nuanced,” Naikal said. “It could be circumstances and instances that they would choose to go one way or the other. Our idea with the software is to give them a starting point on the research and on where to go look.”

The partnership is a sign that the broader industry is recognizing good repair behavior, he adds. Shops that bring vehicles back to the factory state of safety will be rewarded for that behavior, he says.
“This is a good thing that the broader industry is starting to recognize shops that go the extra mile and make sure that the cars are repaired correctly,” Naikal says.

During a Collision Industry Conference meeting earlier this year, Rebekah Cooper, The Cooper Firm partner, explained how improper repairs, including those that involve ADAS systems, can be deadly or cause serious injuries.

Improper repair cases are changing as more emerging technology, such as ADAS features, become prominent on vehicles, she said. She said the legal system currently sees dozens of ADAS cases annually and that number is expected to increase.
She told the story of a case where a repair involving a bumper necessitated a calibration that wasn’t completed by the repair shop.

The firm discovered this by looking at what technology was on the vehicle and the repair procedures to see how it’s supposed to be repaired. They tracked the vehicle back to the last place it was repaired. It was discovered the business didn’t do the needed repair, she said.

The failed repair caused the collision warning not to work, she said. The consumer was quadriplegic following the crash. She lived in a mobile home for three years waiting for accountability, Cooper added.

“There are times we ask a shop for those, and the OEM has it, but the shop does not,” Cooper said. “Have you seen this before? When is the first time? Are you seeing it for the first time right now? If the answer is yes, that’s a problem.”

Intrepid and Kinetic’s new program will also give Intrepid Direct collision repair customers a limited-time free trial of Kinetic ID Premium and provide Kinetic network shops with access to Intrepid Direct insurance.
The program will kick off with Kinetic and Intrepid Direct co-hosting an event at Wynn Las Vegas Tuesday, Nov. 3 at 6 p.m. during the SEMA Show.
The Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ (SCRS) 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit will dive into a conversation about ADAS and calibrations during the SEMA Show next week.

The afternoon begins with “The National Safety Objective: Safer Vehicles, Safer Roads,” featuring National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Deputy Administrator Lee White, who will examine federal vehicle and roadway safety priorities.

The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5 from 12:30-1:30 p.m., will include a conversation about emerging transportation technologies, data-driven research, and the federal government’s work with the industry to reduce fatalities and serious injuries, an SCRS release states.

During the “Engineering the Safety Benefit: From Requirements to Real-World Performance” session, active safety engineers from General Motors and Rivian will provide a look behind the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety before, during, and after a collision.

The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5, from 2–3 p.m., will explore ADAS feature development, real-world effectiveness, crash avoidance and mitigation, implications of inoperable systems, verification of safety performance, and the potential for system degradation.

A session that follows, “Preserving the Driver Assistance System: Sensors, Calibration and Repairability,” will include service engineering experts from General Motors, Ford Motor Co., and Rivian. The conversation will answer for repairers what it takes to preserve and restore ADAS capabilities engineered into the vehicle after collisions.
The session, held Thursday, Nov. 5, from 3:30–4:30 p.m., will also take attendees behind the development of collision repair information.
The 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit is part of SCRS’ Repairer Driven Education (RDE) program at the SEMA Show, which includes several classes, the IDEAS Collide Showcase, and more.

An SCRS RDE Full Series Pass provides access to Tuesday and Wednesday RDE sessions, IDEAS Collide, the OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, and the SCRS Afterparty. To register for the full series pass, click here.
For additional information about SCRS and Repairer Driven Education, visit scrs.com/rde.

articles.title: College Students Build Skills — and a Bronco – At SEMA
articles.author: Matthew Simpson

paras.en: At this year’s SEMA Show, we are turning customization into a live, hands-on experience. Attendees will be able to use the Ford Custom Garage 3D configurator onsite to design their dream Ford Bronco with Ford Accessories and Ford Racing Parts in our inaugural Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build Competition. Then, six Washtenaw Community College (WCC) students will bring the winning design to life on the show floor, building the Bronco live in our booth before it is revealed on the final day of the show.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That show-floor build is the headline moment — and it is also the reason this program matters. Together with WCC, we created a semester-long experience that connects students to real vehicles, current tools, industry leaders, and the business of vehicle customization, giving them a role on one of the biggest stages in the automotive aftermarket.

At Ford, building the future of the automotive industry means investing in more than vehicles. It means investing in the people who will build, customize, service, and improve them. Our Ultimate Build at SEMA makes that investment visible, turning a classroom partnership into a public demonstration of student skill, creativity, and career potential.
A Semester of Learning, Access and Hands-On Work

Across eight weekly sessions from September through October, my Ford colleagues and our industry partners showed students how ideas move from concept to customer — and introduced the careers that make that work possible.

Our Ford Speaker Series covered the aftermarket and dealer business, product development, design, hands-on customization, original equipment manufacturer (OEM) personalization, the business behind Ford Customization and marketing for SEMA. Students heard directly from professionals across design, engineering, accessories, operations, and marketing.

We also loaned two Bronco SUVs and gave tools to the class, which made these lessons tangible. With guidance from instructors and working professionals, students inspected, diagnosed, disassembled, installed, and problem-solved on real vehicles — the kind of experience that connects classroom learning to the work happening every day across the industry.
The Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build at SEMA

At SEMA, our Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build invites attendees to take part in the process. Using an onsite 3D configurator, they can build their dream Ford Bronco. A panel will select 10 finalists, the public will vote for the winning design, and WCC students will build it live in our booth before revealing the completed Bronco to the public on the show’s final day.

The live build gives students a national stage, but it also gives them a demanding real-world assignment. Working on a compressed timeline, the students will draw on a semester of technical training and conversations about product development, design, personalization, business, and marketing.

SEMA is the capstone, not the whole story. The real value is in the preparation that gets them there — the technical practice, the exposure to working professionals and the confidence that comes from contributing to a vehicle thousands of people will see at SEMA.
“At Ford, building the future means investing in the people behind our vehicles, not just the vehicles themselves.”
Matt Simpson, Executive Director of Ford Customization

Our country faces a significant skilled-trades gap. According to a new report, “The Alliance for America’s Skilled-Trades: A National Report,” supported by BlackRock, Carhartt, Ford, and Google, more workers in the United States are aging out of skilled-trades jobs than are entering. Data shows that 24% of the trades workforce nationally is 55 or over and nearing an exit, while just 11% of workers are under 25.

Many young people value hands-on careers but do not always know what opportunities exist or how to enter these fields. This program helps close that distance by combining instruction, equipment, industry exposure, and a national platform where students can demonstrate their skills.
At Ford, we cannot close that gap alone, but we can work with strong educational partners to put vehicles and resources in students’ hands and connect training to real customer and business needs.

The six students were selected through a competitive application process, and they bring interests ranging from collision repair and refinishing to electrical systems, performance upgrades, custom fabrication, and mechanical engineering. They represent a broader WCC learning community that participated in the semester’s classes, vehicle work, and speaker sessions.

The winning Bronco will show more than how a Bronco can be customized. It will show what students can accomplish when they have access to real vehicles, current tools, relevant instruction, and working professionals who can help connect their skills to future careers.

At Ford Customization, and across the entire Ford Customer Service Division, we believe the customer relationship does not end when someone buys a Ford; it is just the start of the journey to make it their Ford. The relationship continues through the parts, accessories, service, and expertise that help owners make their vehicles work better for their lives.

Ford Custom Garage is one expression of that work, making personalization easier through Ford-engineered, tested and warranty-backed packages — but skilled people bring those packages to life. Our WCC partnership connects both sides: donated Broncos and tools support instruction, guest lecturers explain the work behind customization, and SEMA gives students a chance to apply their skills in public.

When the completed Bronco is revealed, the most important result will not only be the vehicle itself. It will be the learning behind it: new skills, professional relationships and a clearer view of the careers open to these students.

They are why we are investing in this program. They represent the talent and craftsmanship our industry needs and what is possible when education and industry work together to create sustained access to the skills, people, and opportunities that turn potential into a career.

articles.title: How Do We Recruit the Next Generation of Technicians?
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: The automotive industry faces a growing workforce challenge, making automotive technician recruitment increasingly important for repair shops. A wave of experienced technicians is nearing retirement, while the number of incoming workers is not large enough to replace them.
The industry needs tens of thousands of jobs filled each year. At the same time, training programs are not producing enough graduates, and Americans are keeping their vehicles longer.
Shops looking to close the labor gap need to reach the next generation of workers earlier and more effectively.
Automotive Technician Recruitment Can Reach New Candidates
Recruiting the next generation of technicians starts with reaching candidates where they are. That can include groups shops may not traditionally consider, such as recent college graduates.

Many young people are leaving college and entering a crowded job market. Some graduates may be open to different career paths, particularly those offering competitive pay, stability and an in-demand skill.
Employee-sponsored training and formal apprenticeship programs can help provide that path.
Job Postings Should Explain the Purpose of the Work

Younger workers also want to understand the purpose behind their work. They want to know who they are helping and why their role matters. For that reason, job postings should communicate more than the availability of an automotive technician position.

Cars are part of everyday life, and technicians help keep people moving. Shops are hiring employees who play a role in keeping vehicles on the road. Communicating that purpose can help candidates understand the broader value of the job.
Workplace Culture Can Support Technician Retention

Many young workers are accustomed to having options and experiencing rapid change. If a workplace does not meet their expectations, they may choose to leave rather than remain in the position. That makes workplace culture an important part of technician recruitment and retention.

Shops can build stronger relationships by taking an interest in employees’ lives and creating opportunities for teams to connect. Team events can also help employees become more comfortable with one another and feel more connected to the shop.

articles.title: Don’t Forget Lubrication During an Oil Change
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Back in my day at the service station, when a customer came in for an oil change, they pulled it into a grease pit and we would grease up everything on the vehicle—ball joints, universal joints, and then we would do the oil changes. Today, it’s different. Vehicles are a lot more low maintenance.

However, the aftermarket has not abandoned the message that lubrication is required for certain repair components to make that repair just that much better. In other words, we have ball joints that have grease nipples that need to be lubricated every so often, like during an oil change. It’s also written in the vehicle service information that doors and lift hatches need to be lubricated every so often.
Your shop probably has an oil change and you probably call it an LOF. So let’s put that L back in LOF: lubrication, oil, filter.
This video is sponsored by Auto Value and Bumper To Bumper.

articles.title: Magnaflow President Dan Paolone on the ‘Long-Term Play’
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: This episode of DriveTime features Dan Paolone, president of Magnaflow.

Paolone said Magnaflow’s family-owned heritage has shaped both its culture and its long-term approach to the market. Founded in 1981 by his uncle, Jerry Paolone, the company has operated around a “build it and stand by it” philosophy while emphasizing lasting relationships and accountability from design through manufacturing. While Magnaflow is widely associated with performance exhaust, Paolone emphasized that the company is fundamentally an emissions and exhaust business, with approximately 10,000 SKUs across catalytic converters and BRExhaust. That breadth, combined with its premium performance brands, gives Magnaflow a much broader aftermarket presence than its performance reputation alone might suggest, he explained.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Vertical integration is another key part of Magnaflow’s strategy. Paolone said the company invests consistently in employees, infrastructure and capital to maintain greater control from research and development through manufacturing and distribution. That approach also extends to data, an area where Magnaflow has made significant investments. By controlling more of the process and supply chain, Paolone said the company gains flexibility while supporting its long-term strategy. That philosophy reflects Magnaflow’s broader approach to business: Rather than managing quarter to quarter, the company views each quarter as another step toward executing a plan measured in years and decades.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Looking ahead, Paolone sees significant growth opportunities across Magnaflow’s existing emissions and exhaust business, BRExhaust and its expanding OE business. The company models vehicle trends through 2040 and expects hybrids, which still require catalytic converters and exhaust systems, to create additional opportunities. BRExhaust is also expanding by offering complete installation kits for repair shops that eliminate the need for welding, cutting or pipe bending, helping technicians complete more repairs in-house. On the OE side, Magnaflow sees an opportunity to serve lower-volume platforms, particularly vehicles in the 10,000- to 20,000-unit range, where its infrastructure and consumer-facing brand can make it an attractive partner.

articles.title: MEYLE German License Plate Fundraiser to Return to AAPEX
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: MEYLE announced that it will bring its German license plate fundraiser to raise money for Northwood University scholarships back to AAPEX 2026 (Nov. 3-5 in Las Vegas).

MEYLE will host the fundraiser at its exhibit at the show, featuring a German license plate stamping machine. Visitors can create custom MEYLE-branded plates in exchange for donations benefiting Northwood students.
Last year’s initiative generated $9,171 in donations. MEYLE supplemented that amount with a $5,000 matching contribution, bringing the total to $14,171.
Northwood Student Receives First MEYLE Scholarship

Earlier this year, Quinn Balcam became the first recipient of the MEYLE scholarship. Balcam, an automotive aftermarket management major from Bloomington, Indiana, serves as president of Northwood’s student aftermarket club.

MEYLE notes that Balcam has demonstrated his industry commitment through multiple internships and leadership in the Northwood University International Auto Show’s aftermarket division. He has also participated in events including AAPEX, SEMA and Heavy-Duty Aftermarket Week.

“Seeing the funds raised at AAPEX translate into scholarship support for a student like Quinn illustrates why partnerships like this are so important,” said James O’Dell, director of aftermarket education at Northwood University. “The automotive aftermarket needs talented, motivated young professionals, and MEYLE is helping our students gain both the financial support and industry connections they need to succeed.”

articles.title: Dana to Showcase Drivetrain and Sealing Technology at AAPEX
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Dana Incorporated will showcase its technologies at the Automotive Aftermarket Products Expo (AAPEX) from Nov. 3-5. Featuring the company’s Victor Reinz and Spicer brands, Dana will offer interactive displays highlighting its drivetrain and sealing technologies. Attendees can examine components, see systems in motion and explore how Dana products work together within vehicles.

“AAPEX gives us the opportunity to put our technologies directly in the hands of the people who sell, install and service them,” said Bill Nunnery, senior director, Aftermarket, Americas region at Dana Incorporated. “By inviting visitors to explore these interactive displays, we’re connecting the parts they know with the systems they support. It’s a hands-on look at the engineering expertise, product coverage and technical support behind our brands.”
Dana to Feature Hands-On Technology Displays

A light-vehicle driveline demonstrator featuring Spicer components will illustrate drivetrain operations. Visitors can use a control panel to switch between two-wheel and four-wheel drive. They can watch a rotating driveshaft transfer power through the axles to turn the wheels.

The interactive display highlights the relationship among driveshafts, universal joints and ring-and-pinion technologies. It gives attendees a closer look at Dana components typically hidden beneath a vehicle.

An engine display with exposed layers will showcase Victor Reinz sealing products and their placement between engine surfaces. Visitors can explore how these components fit within the engine assembly. Additional displays will feature light-vehicle and commercial-vehicle gaskets, ranging from original equipment designs to aftermarket repair solutions.
Engineering Expertise Across the Portfolio

Victor Reinz product displays will highlight Dana’s engineering approach, including Wave Stopper head gasket technology and MeshGuard intake manifold gaskets. The displays will also feature valve covers to support complete repairs. The assortment will showcase the brand’s gasket portfolio, original equipment quality standards and coverage across domestic, European import and commercial-vehicle applications.

The booth will also feature products from Dana’s 2026 portfolio expansion. The expansion introduced more than 500 Victor Reinz gasket part numbers and 54 Spicer aftermarket part numbers. These additions broaden sealing and drivetrain repair options for light-vehicle and commercial-vehicle applications. They also expand Dana’s aftermarket coverage.
Spicer Displays Highlight Expanded Vehicle Coverage
Spicer displays will showcase drivetrain components supporting expanded coverage for current vehicle platforms, including Ford Super Duty and Jeep applications.
Attendees can visit Dana at booth V2431 on Level 2 of the Venetian Expo from Nov. 3-5. They can explore the displays and discuss product applications and technical resources with the Dana team.

articles.title: Sensata Technologies Names Enrico Manuele Aftermarket VP & GM
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Sensata Technologies announced that Enrico Manuele has joined the company as vice president and general manager of aftermarket. Sensata serves the aftermarket through two customer-facing brands. Schrader TPMS provides tire pressure monitoring solutions, while PRECO Radar provides collision-mitigation solutions for commercial applications.
Manuele Brings Experience to Sensata Technologies
Manuele brings more than 30 years of industry experience and joins Sensata from Bosch Mobility Aftermarket. He most recently held global responsibility for sales and customer growth.
He has led businesses and teams across Europe and North America. He brings extensive industry experience and a global perspective to his new role.

“Enrico’s deep aftermarket expertise, global perspective and strong customer orientation make him well suited to lead this business,” said Markus Schwabe, Executive Vice President and President of Automotive, Sensata Technologies. “His experience leading teams across Europe and North America will help us strengthen execution, deepen customer relationships and pursue new growth opportunities worldwide.”

Manuele’s appointment supports Sensata’s continued focus on aftermarket customers, operations and growth. The company plans to build on its brands’ established market presence and customer relationships.

“I am excited to join Sensata and lead its Aftermarket business,” said Manuele. “I look forward to working with our teams, customers and partners around the world to build on the strength of our brands, deepen customer relationships and create new opportunities for growth.”

articles.title: Clarios Announces Plans to Acquire Ecobat
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Clarios announced plans to acquire Ecobat, including the company’s three U.S. critical mineral recovery and processing facilities. Clarios manufactures low-voltage automotive batteries and advanced energy storage solutions. The proposed acquisition would preserve and strengthen domestic critical mineral processing and recovery capacity amid growing demand and supply chain concerns. By integrating these facilities into its circular supply network, Clarios aims to recover, process and return valuable materials to U.S. manufacturers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Clarios Acquisition Includes Three U.S. Facilities

The proposed acquisition includes three critical mineral recovery facilities in City of Industry, California; Indianapolis; and Middletown, New York. The transaction also includes Ecobat’s Dallas office. Together, these facilities currently process more than 40 million batteries annually, recovering lead, tin, antimony and other materials.
The companies expect to close the transaction by early 2027, pending customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals.

“As a world leader in critical minerals processing and recovery, Clarios is uniquely positioned to strengthen this highly capable U.S. recycling operation supported by an experienced workforce,” said Clarios CEO Mark Wallace. “We see a significant opportunity to build on Ecobat’s foundation by evaluating opportunities for future investment in these operations and supporting the continued success of the business. Together, these facilities will strengthen domestic critical mineral recycling capacity, enhance supply chain security, and support the U.S. manufacturing base for years to come.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As part of the transition, Clarios will maintain and build upon Ecobat’s environmental, health and safety practices across the acquired facilities. Following closing, Clarios will combine the best practices of both organizations. The company said this approach aligns with its commitment to responsible operations and local communities.

Clarios and Ecobat intend to work closely with employees, union representatives and regulators throughout the review and transition process. They will focus on operational continuity, environmental compliance, workforce stability and long-term investment in U.S. critical mineral processing and recovery capacity.

“I am proud of what our North American team has built. These facilities are vital to the country’s supply of recycled critical minerals, and our team has earned an industry-recognized record of safety and environmental performance,” said Tom Slabe, Ecobat president and CEO. “Clarios has made a public commitment to investing in U.S. recycling capacity, and that makes it the right owner for the next chapter. This transaction completes the strategic initiative we announced with the earlier sale of our European operations, and it delivers a strong outcome for Ecobat’s stakeholders.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Acquisition Would Expand Battery Recycling Capacity

Clarios operates closed-loop battery processing and recovery systems. The company collects used batteries, recovers critical materials and manufactures new batteries using recycled content. The proposed acquisition would strengthen Clarios’ closed-loop model, expand access to critical materials and improve domestic battery supply chain resilience.

The transaction also represents an investment in the U.S. industrial base and workforce while supporting domestic supply chain independence. Recycled lead batteries represent the country’s largest domestic source of recovered critical minerals. These include antimony, lead and tin, which support defense and advanced technology applications.
Investment Supports U.S. Manufacturing Strategy

The investment advances Clarios’ broader $6 billion U.S. Energy Manufacturing Strategy. That strategy includes a $1.9 billion commitment to strengthen domestic critical mineral recycling and processing capabilities.

The proposed acquisition would preserve existing recycling infrastructure while creating opportunities for future expansion. Clarios will continue evaluating opportunities to expand its capabilities across the United States.
Ecobat Completes Portfolio Transformation

The sale marks the final step in a portfolio transformation Ecobat began in 2025. Over approximately 16 months, the company completed 10 divestitures spanning 17 sites across six countries. These transactions included the sale of its European operations. The proposed sale of its North American platform to Clarios would conclude that transformation.

articles.title: Think Twice Before Erasing Trouble Codes
articles.author: Counterman Staff

paras.en: Counter pros should avoid erasing diagnostic trouble codes when customers request it. Clearing codes without fixing the underlying problem will only temporarily turn off the check engine light.

Erasing codes also deletes valuable freeze-frame data that technicians need for accurate diagnosis. Additionally, clearing codes resets emissions readiness monitors, potentially affecting vehicle emissions testing.
This video is sponsored by The Pronto Network.

articles.title: Standard Motor Products Expands Climate Control Portfolio
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Standard Motor Products, Inc. (SMP), through its Temperature Control Division and flagship Four Seasons brand, has introduced a comprehensive line of A/C condensers engineered to meet OE performance specifications across a broad range of foreign name plate and domestic vehicles, the company said.

The new line is backed by more than 100 years of experience serving the automotive aftermarket. Engineered to OE dimensional fit and thermal performance specifications, Four Seasons A/C condensers deliver the quality and reliability professional technicians expect while helping distributors and repair facilities simplify inventory management, SMP said.

Each condenser is manufactured as a direct-fit replacement with OE-style construction and cooling capacity to support proper system performance and efficient installation. Units include the required sealing components for a complete, leak-free installation and are packaged to protect critical heat-exchanger fins and connections during shipping and handling.

With the addition of A/C condensers, customers can source complete A/C system repair solutions from a single, trusted supplier, according to SMP. The Four Seasons climate control portfolio includes new and remanufactured compressors, evaporators, accumulators, receiver driers, expansion devices, hoses and repair kits.

“Adding premium A/C condensers to the Four Seasons portfolio reinforces our commitment to providing complete thermal management solutions for professional installers,” said Jack Ramsey, senior vice president of sales and marketing at Standard Motor Products. “With OE-engineered performance, extensive application coverage and a full range of HVAC components from a single source, we are helping distribution partners reduce complexity and giving technicians confidence in every repair.”

articles.title: Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
articles.author: Olivia Maule

paras.en: Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.

The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.

And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?
Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.

The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.
One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.

Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.

The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.

To understand why negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction — a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.

In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.

Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.

When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.

This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.
The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.
What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.
That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.

Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.

Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.

Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.

In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.

For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."
How Neanderthal and human groups interacted

Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.

"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."
Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.

Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.

"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."

At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.

Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.

Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.

In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.

While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.
In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.

Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."

Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.

Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?

Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.

Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.

Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.
The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.
"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.

In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."

His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.

Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.

That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.

We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry our ancestral populations eroded quickly.

Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.

paras.en: "That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."

Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.

Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.
If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?

Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.

The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.

In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.

paras.en: "We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.

Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.

There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.
If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events — but they don't.

As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.

Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.
"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.

It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.

Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.
The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.

The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.

paras.en: - 'More Neanderthal than human': How your health may depend on DNA from our long-lost ancestors
- Early Homo sapiens may have lived in rainforests, new clues suggest — and it could overturn our understanding of human evolution
- Scientists show that DNA can last for up to 50,000 years in Africa — much longer than previously thought
"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."
However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.

The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.
"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. articles.title: Decapitated man buried near fort in Roman-era Scotland gets a new virtual face
articles.author: Tom Metcalfe

paras.en: Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other headless bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.
Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.
"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.
The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.
- The Romans and Vikings left few genetic traces of their occupations of Britain, research suggests
- Case of mysterious medieval skeleton buried in Roman-era sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey finally solved
- 'It's a portrait of their actual ancestor': Facial reconstruction of Indigenous man who lived in Ecuador 3,000 years ago shared with his descendants

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.
What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

articles.title: 'This is so crazy!' Virginia college student looking for shark teeth finds rare Native American spearpoint
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

"Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement. Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled.

The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period.

The field trip was part of an ecology course led by Mary Baldwin University faculty members who had secured a permit from the state to explore the barrier islands off the Eastern Shore, the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula that includes most of Delaware and parts of Virginia and Maryland.

Just after a lunch break on Sept. 21, the last day of the excursion that aimed to let students study plants and animals in the coastal ecosystem, Rolph set out to quickly explore a mound of shells on the island and noticed the spearpoint at the edge of an inlet. Her professors were blown away by the lucky discovery.

"The set of circumstances that came together that made this possible is quite unbelievable," Paul Callo, a biology professor at Mary Baldwin University who was co-leading the trip, said in the statement. "The tide was coming in, so the spear point was soon to be buried."
When Rolph showed Callo the artifact, he was "truly at a loss for words," he said. "It is certainly awe-inspiring to see and touch something that was made by human hands thousands of years ago."

The barrier island where Rolph found the stone point is part of a natural area owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, which means the artifact is now the property of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Archaeologists collected it from the Mary Baldwin group and have taken it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.
Rolph was fine with not keeping the spearpoint. "That's how you get cursed!" she said.
How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz!

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
