paras.en: Keep calm, carry on… and keep a warship at the ready.
You're going to see everything… including earnings and guidance.
The next few days are critical for energy investors. Earnings roll out from ExxonMobil (XOM), Chevron (CVX), Marathon Petroleum (MPC), and ConocoPhillips (COP).
I'll just be blunt: these numbers are going to be big. Texas-sized big.

The expected numbers for ExxonMobil, Chevron, and ConocoPhillips are above. All three are expected to more than double of EPS from last year. Then there are the refining-heavy companies. Those are a different thing altogether.

Marathon Petroleum's earnings estimate is $25.37 a share. That's not a typo. Three months ago, EPS came in at $17.73, versus an estimate of "only" $14.27. And consider this: just one year ago, the Ohio-based company earned $4.51 per share. The jump in oil prices and - more importantly - the huge "crack spread" on refined products have sales expected to increase by $13 billion in just one year.

For all four, guidance may be more important than the earnings themselves. What these companies say about the future and capital spending matters most. Any changes to spending plans will be closely watched by investors.

These numbers are also likely to be closely watched by the political class. They are likely to use these big numbers to excoriate the industry as oil prices rise. An industry source tells me that the industry is "used to" the political attacks, but wishes there were more focus on the boom-or-bust nature of much of the industry, and that the money these firms earn now will help brace against the bad times and when - not if - oil drops again at some point in the future.
Whatever your bent is on Big Oil, get the popcorn ready, because the next week will be big for all you energy investors - in many ways - and hopefully you'll see everything.

For investors, caution is warranted on the energy space, says BTIG's chart analyst Jonathan Krinksy. On refiners specifically, he notes that the S&P Refining Index is up nearly 160% in 2026, its best year in at least three decades by far.
"At a minimum we should expect consolidation, but more likely some significant downside reversion," wrote Krinsky earlier this week.
Krinsky doesn't like the look of the charts on Valero and Marathon Petroleum. On the latter, the analyst said the stock "hasn't quite broken its uptrend, but feels like it's coming."

This week, we spoke with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright. He joined us from a nuclear power plant in rural Illinois. His office is offering billions of dollars in loan guarantees to help build out more nuclear power capacity in the U.S. We spoke with the secretary about that, as well as oil, Iran, Hormuz, and the importance of U.S. LNG in keeping Europe running right now.

articles.title: Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan

paras.en: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment of a candidate named Dan Sullivan for the state's U.S. Senate race, where the incumbent shares the same name, violated criminal or civil laws.

Dunleavy's order late Wednesday was in response to a report by The New York Times Wednesday that people in the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and senior advisors at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee worked to recruit retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run to draw votes from Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The incumbent senator, like Dunleavy, is a Republican.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, in response to the Times article, said they are not involved in the campaign of the retired teacher Sullivan.

The governor's order came as a federal judge in Alaska allowed Peltola's campaign and the DSCC to intervene in a U.S. Justice Department lawsuit that seeks to block the state from immediately certifying any Senate election result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The campaign, the DSCC and state election officials have asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss that lawsuit before Election Day, Nov. 3.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit.
The political stakes in the Alaska Senate race are potentially momentous. The winner of the contest could determine the balance of power in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-vote majority.

Dunleavy, in announcing his order, noted that Alaska's Division of Elections had investigated concerns that the retired teacher's entry into the Senate primary was designed to confuse voters, which led the division to block him from that ballot. A state court judge reversed that order, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling, allowing him on the ballot.
"The new reporting substantially supports the Division's findings," Dunleavy said in a post on X.

"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," Dunleavy said. "The evidence will determine what happens next."

"Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," he said. "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.

Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on Thursday in response to Dunleavy's announcement, said, "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight. The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

Gleason late Wednesday ordered the DOJ to respond by late Thursday afternoon to motions to dismiss its lawsuit by Peltola's campaign, the DSCC, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and the advocacy group Common Cause, whom the judge also had allowed to intervene in the case.
Gleason said those groups needed to file any response to the DOJ's response by early Friday afternoon.

Trump, before flying to South Carolina for a campaign rally Thursday morning, was asked by a reporter whether Republicans in the Senate should try to block Peltola from taking the seat in January if she wins Tuesday's election.
"Well, you're going to have to see what happens," Trump said.
"It's hard to believe that she can even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run," the president said.
Trump said the retired teacher Sullivan "was just put there as a fraud."
"But people aren't going to know that, so nobody's going to know what to do," Trump said.
Both Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have argued that Trump and other Republicans are being hypocritical in their claims about the Senate race.

"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said Wednesday.
The DSCC pointed to instances of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.

Alaska elections officials in a court filing have said the Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
The retired teacher's name on the ballot is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as "Sullivan, Dan. S." with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Alaska elections officials said in their court filing that "the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate."

articles.title: Mathematicians find an infinite number of Ramanujan equations

paras.en: The legendary mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and Yifeng Huang, a postdoctoral researcher at Emory University, have something in common: they will not be ignored. In 1912 Ramanujan, a 24-year-old clerk at what was then the Madras Port Trust in India, began mailing pages of new, unproven formulas to mathematicians across England. One of his letters eventually reached British mathematician G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who recognized Ramanujan as a visionary, invited him to visit and helped launch his groundbreaking career.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: More than a century later, Huang, while a graduate student at the University of Michigan, began e-mailing mathematicians letter after letter—more than 40 in total. He scarcely heard back.

Huang’s ideas concerned two formulas that appeared in Ramanujan’s letters and are now known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. In September 2026 Huang and a few collaborators uploaded a proof that the historic equations represent a single case of a much grander geometrical theory. In particular, the work showed that the Roger-Ramanujan identities correspond to a trefoil knot in a certain space. The trefoil, known as the shape of the familiar Celtic knot, is one of the simplest mathematical knots. And related knots, they found, reveal an infinite number of previously unknown identities.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“Everything about this subject, even the original discovery, is a surprise,” says George Andrews, a mathematician at Pennsylvania State University and an expert on Ramanujan’s math. Ramanujan, Hardy and their collaborators “were all unable to prove this,” he adds. “So the things that have cropped up from knot theory were a total surprise to me.”

Hardy was responsible for shaping much of early 20th century number theory. Initially skeptical when he received a letter from Ramanujan, Hardy later wrote that he recognized the letter’s author as “a mathematician of the highest quality, a man of altogether exceptional originality and power.” It was a pivotal moment.

Two of Ramanujan’s formulas were startling: they represented an infinite series of sums on one side and an infinite series of products on the other, with no visible reason for the two to agree. By 1916 British mathematician Percy MacMahon had found a way to read them. These two equations were similar to ones studied two centuries earlier by mathematician Leonhard Euler. Euler had a neat trick for sidestepping such complexity: he connected the equations to a type of counting problem known as a “partition.” A partition of a number is a way of writing it as a sum. MacMahon transformed Ramanujan’s formulas into two kinds of partitions that looked nothing alike, but whose counts always came out identical.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Here’s how one side of a Ramanujan equation was partitioned: count the number of ways to sum up to a certain value using numbers that are at least two whole numbers apart. For instance, 6 can be written as 1 + 5, 2 + 4 and 6. So there are three partitions.
On the other side, sum using only numbers that end in 1, 4, 6 or 9. For 6, the answer is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 4 and 6, which also gives three partitions.

The formulas say these two very different counts agree for every number. Before Ramanujan could prove them, he came across an obscure proof by English mathematician Leonard James Rogers in an old math journal. Thus, the equations became known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
“It was regarded, for most of the 20th century, as an isolated gem,” Andrews says. No one suspected it lay at the heart of a much larger theory.

In the early 1970s Andrews uncovered an infinite family of the identities. “I discovered them only to learn that [mathematician] Basil Gordon had done them first,” Andrews says, “which was a huge disappointment for me.”
The new family came to be known as the Andrews-Gordon identities.

Since then the identities have turned up in strange places: in representation theory, in the study of symmetric functions, even in physics via the “hard hexagon model,” which describes how gas atoms can settle onto a surface in a triangular pattern.
“Who would have thought that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities were related to how liquid helium behaves when poured onto a graphite plate?” Andrews says.

Matrices—little spreadsheets of numbers—can undergo operations such as flips and transpositions, which must be done in a certain order to get the correct result. But if the values of the matrices are chosen such that the order of operations doesn’t matter (meaning they “commute”), then the matrices behave like coordinates and can be used to describe curves. Take any smooth curve, such as the parabola y = x2, and replace y and x with pairs of matrices. A textbook-level problem might ask: How many pairs of matrices make the equation true? A math student can find the answer.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But what happens if you use a curve that isn’t so smooth—one that has a “pinch” in it, also known as a singularity? Now textbook theory breaks down. These matrix counts had neverbeen studied.

While he was still a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, Huang started counting matrices on pinched curves such as y2 = x3, which comes to a sharp tip when x and y equal 0. Before long, his counts reproduced a familiar formula: one side of the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. “Already this discovery is fascinating,” Huang says. “I’m wondering what is going on. It can’t be a coincidence.”

From that single example, Huang made a bold, vague guess: What if every pinched curve hid a new identity, with its matrix count collapsing into a neat formula? Hoping to discuss the idea further, Huang wrote letters to a small group of mathematicians—around five to 10 people.
University of Virginia mathematician Ken Ono received one of those letters. But thinking Huang’s idea was “crazy,” Ono dismissed it.

Another letter recipient was Alexei Oblomkov, a mathematician at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, whose work connects algebraic geometry and knot theory. “I thought it was kind of a great idea, and later we met at one of the conferences, and I liked the idea even more,” Oblomkov says.
By then, Huang and Ruofan Jiang, now a mathematician at the University of California, Berkeley, had devised a systematic way to count how many matrices make the formulas for pinched curves true.

Oblomkov brought geometry to the table. Zoom in on the pinch in y2 = x3, he advised, and surround it with a tiny sphere in four dimensions, where mathematicians say such curves naturally live. The curve pierces the sphere along a closed loop in a “trefoil” knot. Both counts lead to the classic Rogers-Ramanujan identities. What about another curve? It also led to another knot, which was hiding another family of identities. And another curve led to yet more.

The team’s ideas crystalized into the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov (HJO) conjecture. Simply stated, pick any two numbers a and b that are greater than 1, with no common factor. The conjecture predicts that for the curve xa = yb, a count of the matrix solutions will always collapse into a Rogers-Ramanujan-type identity. This translates into infinitely many families of identities, one for every value of a. The case a = 2 is the family Andrews and Gordon found. Every larger value of a was uncharted. And each curve comes with its own knot: the trefoil for a = 2 and b = 3 and more intricately wound torus knots for the rest.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Again, Huang began sending out e-mails—more than 40 in 2023—and gave a circuit of seminar talks.
This time, when Ono received one of Huang’s letters, he found the idea “mind-blowing,” he says. “That’s when I joined this chase.”

By then Ono had signed on to the artificial intelligence company Axiom Math as its founding mathematician. He, Huang and another Axiom mathematician, Kenny Lau, worked for seven months in tandem with AxiomProver, the company’s math-focused AI system.

Because the ideas were so new, Ono says, they couldn’t simply ask an AI model to solve the problem—there was no literature for it to learn from. Instead AxiomProver worked like a research assistant, testing a far more expansive space of ideas than would be humanly possible. It also translated the proof into Lean, a machine-friendly language for automated proof checking. In the end, the quartet made of humans and AI stitched together ideas from five different areas of math to prove the conjecture.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Ono’s take on AI in math is more hopeful than many in his field. “Everyone talks about the end of math,” he says. “But someone had to invent this structure. This is what we should be doing.”
The team members posted their HJO conjecture to the preprint server arXiv.org in August 2026. And in September, the three followed up with the conjecture’s proof.
Recast as geometry, the old identities now point toward unmapped territory, raising questions that mathematicians are eager to explore.

“We found something exciting,” Oblomkov says, “a way to extend the geometry in the case when it’s not a trefoil knot, but a so-called Hopf link—basically you have two circles tied together. So that will be the next paper.”

Oblomkov also says Fields Medalist Peter Scholze has published a few papers that take some of Huang’s ideas even further. The pinched curves xa = yb are only the beginning. The equation is, Huang says, “only the first example of a singularity I would write down.” Oblomkov agrees: “It’s just the first case, and there will be many more.”

articles.title: Five things you need to know about the Trump administration’s rollback of methane regulations

paras.en: The Trump administration has taken an axe to environmental regulations—and this week the target became methane gas emissions.

The White House plans to slash laws governing how much methane is emitted from oil and gas wells. This includes relaxing rules around flaring—or burning off excess natural gas at well sites—as well as doing away with a program that requires speedy fixes for large methane leaks. The move also lowers standards for marginal wells, which produce little oil and gas but are responsible for about half of the industry’s methane emissions.

It’s the latest bump in a regulator roller coaster for methane. Attempts to regulate emissions on a federal level began in 2015, when the Obama administration sought to bring methane under the Clean Air Act. The first Trump administration rolled back that rule change. Then, during the Biden administration, the then Democratic-controlled Congress reinstated the methane regulations and cleared the way for the Environmental Protection Agency to apply the new standards to older equipment. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act also included provisions for charges for heavy emitters and allocated money for both industry and research to help them comply with the rules.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

All of that again went out the window with the second Trump administration. As the latest changes start to take effect, here are five things you need to know about methane and the ways that these moves will affect you.
Methane is a major driver of climate change

Carbon dioxide may be more prevalent in the atmosphere, but methane is a heavy hitter, climate-wise. The gas has been responsible for about 30 percent of the rise in global temperatures since the start of the industrial revolution, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for about 12 years, while an excess carbon dioxide molecule can persist for centuries. But methane traps heat about 80 times more effectively than carbon over 20 years and about 28 times more effectively over the course of a century. In other words, it may be shorter lived, but the damage methane does while it’s in the atmosphere is greater.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Oil and gas leaks are a major source of methane

Each year, according to the IEA, about 580 million metric tons of methane enter the atmosphere. About 40 percent of this comes from natural sources such as swamp gas and volcanic emissions. The other 60 percent comes from human sources.

Agriculture is the biggest contributor to this anthropogenic portion of methane emissions, but the combination of natural gas and petroleum production, processing and transportation comes in second. These processes are responsible for 28 percent of all U.S. methane emissions, according to the EPA.
Methane regulations have done little to move the needle

With all the regulatory back-and-forth, it’s perhaps unsurprising that research into methane emissions finds little evidence that federal rules make a difference. In a recent paper in Communications Earth & Environment, Johns Hopkins University associate professor of environmental health and engineering Scot Miller and his colleagues used satellite data to track emissions independently.
“Overall,” Miller says, “you see this landscape across the U.S. where methane leaks from oil and gas facilities are declining, but it’s not necessarily due to any kind of concerted federal action.”

Methane emissions declined by about 11 percent between 2019 and 2024, but the decline was caused by technological changes in the industry and the establishment of new natural gas pipelines that can carry methane to market—without this transport system, operators often burn off natural gas at well sites.
“If [natural gas is] actually a valuable markable product, there is evidence to show that leak rates tend to go down,” Miller explains.
The new rules would loosen restrictions on the most common oil wells in the U.S.

The new changes are twofold. First, the EPA plans to eliminate the Super Emitter Program, which would have allowed third parties to monitor oil and gas operations for leaks, via satellite, for example, and alert the EPA to leaks of 100 kilograms of methane or more per hour. Operators notified by the EPA of such large leaks would then have to investigate the leaks within days.

The Super Emitter Program has actually never been in effect, so this will make little immediate difference. “This is like the nail in the coffin,” Miller says. “These rules are already not being implemented.”

The other change would affect marginal oil and gas wells. These are wells that produce 15 barrels (2,384 liters) or less of oil per day or 90,000 cubic feet (2,549 cubic meters) or less of natural gas per day over a yearlong period. These wells accounted for 7 percent of U.S. oil and gas production as of 2021, according to the EPA, but produce about 50 percent of the industry’s methane emissions. They’re also plentiful, accounting for more than 70 percent of onshore oil and gas wells.
Each marginal well produces only a little profit, so operators may not have much incentive to invest in repairs and upgrades, Miller says.

“Methane leaks from the oil and gas industry have been declining over time, but these marginal wells are arguably a stubborn outlier,” Miller says. “The regulations proposed during the Biden administration would have helped address this issue.” But they may never come to pass now.
There is broad pushback against regulating methane

Biden administration rules to regulate methane, enacted in 2023, were expected to keep 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tons) of the gas out of the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038. Their rollback is part of a broad push against methane mitigation, however. “I think, potentially, this move would make it more difficult for a future administration to reimplement emissions regulations,” Miller says.

In the European Union, a 2024 regulation would have required methane monitoring and reporting on any imported oil, natural gas and coal. But this month, the European Parliament voted to approve a three-year delay on that regulation.

In another possible blow for methane reduction, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate plans to take up in November, would bar agencies from revoking permits issued during the Trump administration to drill on public land and would make it harder for future administrations to require methane leak monitoring or limits on flaring on public land.
“It’s difficult to have an effective or a consistent federal regulatory policy if those regulations are constantly seesawing up and down,” Miller says.
Disclosure: The reporter’s spouse is employed in the oil and gas industry and owns interests in wells.

articles.title: Scientists can now rewire living brains

paras.en: The human brain holds around 86 billion neurons, wired together in a vast web of hundreds of trillions of connections. These connections, bridged by structures called synapses, form circuits responsible for everything we feel, perceive and do. And they constantly shift as we grow, learn, make memories and form habits.

Neuroscientists have long sought to hack into these circuits to understand how the brain works. Just 20 years ago they developed a technique called optogenetics, which offered some of the first glimpses of these circuits in action—it uses light to turn cells, including brain cells, on and off.

The work won three scientists the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. If brain pathways were highways, optogenetics would be akin to “controlling the volume of traffic on a road network that’s already built,” says Sangkyu Lee, a neurobiologist at the Institute for Basic Science in South Korea.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Better yet, however, would be “changing the structure of the ‘road’ itself,” Lee says—by actually editing the brain’s connections. More recently, scientists have figured out how to add new connections and delete existing ones, and they have used these techniques to change animals’ behavior and even to implant memories. Ultimately, these tools could yield discoveries about the brain and potentially even treatments for psychiatric conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The idea that, by manipulating brain activity, you could, in principle, make someone happy or sad, or thirsty or hungry, is incredible when you think about the ramifications,” says Don Arnold, a neurobiologist at the University of Southern California.

Kafui Dzirasa, a psychiatrist at Duke University, stumbled into “synaptic engineering” by accident. He had been trying to develop treatments for psychiatric conditions using brain-machine interfaces to alter neural activity. Electrodes would pick up activity in one brain region and cause a computer to stimulate another—essentially “wiring” the two regions together. But as a potential treatment for mental illness, it was impractical. So Dzirasa began contemplating other ways to connect two disparate brain regions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “We realized that’s what a synapse does, so we thought, ‘Why don't we just create a synapse?’” he says.

Neurobiologists had already developed a way to do this in a creature with a very simple brain: the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. It has only around 300 neurons, making it ideal for neuroscientists to study. In 2014 Ithai Rabinowitch, a neurobiologist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and his colleagues successfully altered the worms’ behavior by rewiring their neural circuits.

The team did this by creating a kind of synapse that passes electrically charged particles between two cells through special protein channels. These proteins are made by genes that are snuck into cells’ DNA using a specially programmed virus. Rabinowitch’s team inserted mouse synapse proteins into the worms, which created artificial connections that didn’t interfere with worms’ existing synapses. The researchers were able to alter a circuit governing the worms’ sense of smell, causing them to avoid an odor they previously found attractive.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This technique has since been used to study neural circuits involved in everything from defecation to learning. In one striking example, another team of researchers used it to rewire a memory. First, they trained worms to prefer a specific temperature. Then they bypassed the memory with an electrical synapse, causing the worms to move toward warmer temperatures instead. “It’s like an inception experiment, where you plant a memory by making an artificial connection,” says that study’s senior author Daniel Colón-Ramos, a cell biologist at the Yale School of Medicine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But could this approach work in the more complex brains of mammals? As brains get bigger and more complicated, the potential for unintended connections is harder to prevent—these can wreak havoc, potentially causing death. “You need to achieve much more control and precision in an animal with billions of neurons,” Colón-Ramos says.

In a study published in May, Dzirasa, Colón-Ramos and their team proved the technique could be done in a mouse. They created synapse proteins that only connected to a specially engineered partner—not to each other or to synapse proteins that were already in the mouse’s brain. They used the tool to connect different cell types in two brain circuits, producing changes in the mice’s behavior.

Some of these behavioral changes offer hints at parallels in human brains. In a study posted to the preprint server bioRxiv last March, Dzirasa and his colleagues tested the tool in mice with a genetic mutation that caused repetitive grooming behaviors reminiscent of OCD. The researchers introduced synapses to bypass the disrupted circuit, which reduced this pathological behavior. “That’s a clear demonstration of the potential power of this in thinking about human diseases,” Dzirasa says.

Researchers have developed other techniques for engineering new connections, too. But some situations may call for the opposite approach: deleting existing connections. For instance, PTSD can cause otherwise innocuous sights or sounds to trigger anxiety. These reactions may stem from connections formed between sensory neurons and “negative emotion” cells in the amygdala.
“It’s tantalizing to think, if you could wipe those synapses out, maybe you’d get rid of this,” Arnold says.

So far, synapse-deleting tools are much less precise than synapse-adding ones. For example, Arnold and his colleagues discovered a technique that degrades proteins that hold synapses together, deleting them from neurons en masse. Last year they expanded this into a toolkit that can delete only inhibitory or only excitatory synapses (which respectively make neurons less or more likely to fire) and that can be activated with light or chemicals.

And in a study in April, Lee and his colleagues described a slightly more precise synapse-deleting tool called Synthetic Trogocytosis, or SynTrogo, which works by recruiting astrocytes, a type of brain cell that prunes synapses naturally. Using special “lock” and “key” proteins to trigger pruning, Lee’s team was able to delete less than a third of specific cell types’ synapses in two parts of mice’s hippocampus, a brain region that is crucial for memory. The remaining connections became stronger, and the mice showed better performance than unedited animals in memory tests. This finding hints at potential applications in neurodevelopmental conditions that involve abnormal connectivity, such as schizophrenia, but also those involving memory impairment, such as dementia.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Having techniques that can delete as well as add synapses “gives much more versatility,” Colón-Ramos says. “You have a gas pedal, but now you also have brakes, so you can do much more.”

Looking ahead, Rabinowitch envisages a day when scientists can construct designer connectomes—entire brains’ worth of custom connections. “You sit by your computer and say, ‘Let’s build this brain,’” he says. “Then it spills out the list of genes you need to introduce into the organism, and you build your synthetic connectome.” Ultimately, this could produce edited animals that perform specific tasks or even artificial life, Rabinowitch says.
We are a long way from these techniques being used in humans. Optogenetics, the 20-year-old, Nobel Prize–winning technology, has only just proven itself safe in trials of human treatments.

To edit human circuits, researchers will have to figure out how to safely deliver DNA across the blood-brain barrier and into neurons. Scientists are working on brain delivery systems, but “that’s a barrier nobody’s really solved yet,” Arnold says. And no one knows how safe these new tools are. “We’re starting to test if human tissue can tolerate them,” Dzirasa says.

And perhaps more critically, researchers need to understand human brain function better before they can usefully intervene. Synaptic engineering may be just what’s needed to figure this out, however. “If you don’t know how something works, you cannot fix it,” Colón-Ramos says. “These tools will lead to the knowledge we need for any aspiration of healing.”

articles.title: A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
articles.author: Allie Skalnik

paras.en: One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.
While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

articles.title: Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

articles.title: Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course
articles.author: Anirban Mukhopadhyay

paras.en: Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

paras.en: The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

articles.title: Scientists Ran 100,000 Simulations of Comets Striking Earth. The Results Are a Surprise.
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: Where did we come from? The answer, many scientists have proposed, is space.

One longstanding theory, hypothesized for over a century, is that life on Earth emerged from fragments of prebiotic chemistry that arrived from the cosmic unknowns, possibly delivered by far-flung comets.

The idea is supported by a growing body of evidence, with scientists detecting signs of organic molecules in comets soaring through space, which hypothetically could seed the ingredients of life on worlds they come into contact with.
But according to new simulations, the chances of this actually happening are so improbable they're bordering on science fiction.
"It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely," says astronomer Richard Anslow from the University of Cambridge.
In a new study in Scientific Reports, Anslow and fellow researchers ran simulations to test what would happen if comets, as hypothesized, did in fact carry prebiotic chemicals to Earth.
In the simulations, they focused on hydrogen cyanide, a 'feedstock' molecule that can help synthesize many of the building blocks of life – including lipids, sugars, nucleobases, and nucleotides.

Not only has hydrogen cyanide regularly been found in comets, but to date it's the only known feedstock molecule that's been found in sufficient abundance in comets observed in the Solar System to be considered prebiotically relevant, with other chemicals (such as cyanoacetylene and cyanogen) being found in much weaker concentrations.

But would a hypothetically fertile payload of hydrogen cyanide, transported safely to Earth aboard a comet, survive the cataclysmic culmination of its journey as its icy spaceship collided with Earth?

Across 100,000 simulations designed to recreate the conditions of Earth's early comet bombardment – during which time over 100,000 comets struck the planet – the researchers found it was exceedingly unlikely.

In 54 percent of simulations, not a single comet strike would have delivered a sufficient quantity of hydrogen cyanide to Earth's land, with comets breaking apart in Earth's atmosphere, losing their chemical payload in the heat of impact (the biggest factor), or striking oceans where any surviving hydrogen cyanide would be diluted.

The other 46 percent of simulations suggest at least one successful comet could have transported enough of the feedstock molecule to the surface, but even these successful deliveries would have offered only a fleeting opportunity for prebiotic chemistry.

Of course, these are only simulations, and the results don't prove that it didn't or couldn't happen, but they suggest that the cometary impact theory is much less likely than we may have realized before now.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," says Anslow.
"We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."
But just because the calculations suggest that life on Earth probably didn't get seeded by chemicals from comets, that doesn't mean the mechanism couldn't have worked on other planets.

Interestingly, the researchers found that Mars actually provides a better fit for the cometary impact hypothesis, with the red planet's thinner atmosphere and lower impact velocities enabling over five times as many successful transports as Earth.
By contrast, Venus's dense atmosphere would eat up most comets outright, even ones measuring several kilometers in diameter.
The findings are reported in Scientific Reports.

articles.title: There's a Curious Link Between Your Childhood Imaginary Friend And an Uncanny Feeling Later in Life
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: If you had an imaginary friend who walked beside you and joined your childhood games, you may have left them behind as you grew up.
Scientists have now found a connection between that childhood experience and the feeling some adults have that someone is nearby, even when they are alone.
The question reaches beyond how we dream up a companion: How do we come to feel that they are sharing our space?
To investigate, researchers turned to adults' childhood memories. They asked people who recalled imaginary friends about their experiences together, including where those companions seemed to stand.
That detail could help explain how an imagined character acquires a felt location beside us, and whether our awareness of our own bodies plays a part.

The team analyzed responses from 185 adults recruited through İzmir University of Economics in Türkiye who reported no psychiatric or neurological diagnoses. Of these, 45 remembered having an imaginary companion.

Everyone completed a questionnaire assessing how often they felt another presence without clear sensory evidence over the previous month. Those who recalled imaginary friends averaged 25.51 points, compared with 20.07 in the other group, on a scale ranging from 15 to 75.
Higher scores meant more frequent reports of these experiences. The difference suggests that adults who remembered imaginary companions were more prone to sensing a presence during that period.

The childhood memories also revealed a spatial pattern. Companions were most often recalled in front of or beside the body. Of 114 distance estimates for directions in which companions had appeared, 76 placed them within 70 centimeters (about 28 inches).

That puts about two-thirds of those estimates inside the study's chosen boundary for the space immediately surrounding the body. Researchers call this peripersonal space: the nearby area we use when reaching, moving and interacting with others.
The researchers propose that imaginary companions may be linked to the way the brain represents the body and its surroundings, giving an imagined social partner a place within that space.
Earlier robot experiments covered by ScienceAlert offer a clue to how bodily signals can contribute to sensing someone nearby.

In those experiments, participants moved their hands while a robot touched their backs. When researchers introduced a brief delay between the movement and the touch, some participants felt another person behind them.
The proposed explanation was that conflicting signals led the brain to attribute sensations arising from the participant's own actions to someone else.

The new study suggests that childhood imaginary companions and adult felt presence may both relate to how we experience our bodies and surrounding space. There is, however, an intriguing difference in where those experiences seem to unfold.
While the imaginary companions were usually recalled in front of or beside the body, earlier research commonly places adult felt presence behind or beside it.

One possibility the researchers raise is that imaginary friends occupy the space suited to face-to-face conversation and play. A presence behind us could involve ambiguous bodily sensations whose source we cannot immediately check by sight. These explanations are hypotheses; the survey didn't directly test them.

The findings also depend on adults' memories. Because the researchers didn't follow children as they grew up, they cannot establish that imaginary companions cause later presence experiences. Most participants were women, everyone was recruited through one university, and the spatial result depended on analytical choices.

Participants knew the study concerned imaginary companions, which may have inflated the association. The authors caution that the effect could be weaker if the study is repeated without revealing its topic during recruitment.
The results don't provide evidence for ghosts. But they do offer a way to investigate how the brain makes us feel like we're sharing a space with someone.
Following children over time could reveal whether a tendency underlying imaginary companionship continues into adulthood, and how that feeling changes as we grow.
The research has been published in Consciousness and Cognition.

articles.title: After 30 Years, FDA Approves First-Ever Drug For a Rare Neurological Disorder
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Alexander disease is a rare genetic neurological disorder that affects less than one in a million people worldwide. It leads to a multitude of problems, including a loss of mobility, seizures, and issues with speech, and it's often fatal.
The disease is caused by a fault in the gene that makes glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).

The fault creates abnormal versions of GFAP, causing the protein to clump into tangles called Rosenthal fibers. These fibers stress brain helper cells called astrocytes, which then become damaged along with the brain's myelin.

Current treatments focus on managing the symptoms of Alexander disease, but after decades of diligent research, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has now approved the first-ever drug to attack the disease directly.

The drug is zilganersen (brand name Zanvastro), and it targets GFAP directly, reducing the amount that the body produces. In clinical trials, this has now been shown to have a positive effect on key characteristics of the disease.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," says neuropathologist Albee Messing, from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, who has been investigating the condition for more than 30 years.
FDA approval was partly secured through a clinical trial involving 54 pediatric and adult patients aged up to 53, across 13 sites in eight countries.
Motor skills were shown to either stabilize or improve for younger participants, while older participants' walking speed held steady compared with a decline in those who received no treatment.

In treatments lasting more than a year, the drug was shown to meet all the required safety standards to get the all-clear from the FDA. Some people experienced side effects, though most were mild or moderate, and serious ones were less common in treated patients than in the control group.

The most common side effects were vomiting, back pain, cough, headache, and pain after the spinal injection. The FDA also warns that some patients developed aseptic meningitis, an inflammation of the lining around the brain and spinal cord.

"[The] approval of Zanvastro begins a new chapter for people living with Alexander disease and their families, who have long faced this relentlessly progressive and often fatal disease with no treatment options," says medical scientist Brett Monia, CEO of Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the company responsible for developing the drug.

It's taken several stages of research to get to this point with Zanvastro. Messing, together with colleagues including neurobiologist Michael Brenner from the University of Alabama at Birmingham, originally worked with mice bred to produce too much GFAP.
When that led to protein clumps in astrocytes, it put researchers on the path to understanding how Alexander disease develops.
The mouse models were initially designed to overexpress the GFAP gene, and the researchers were surprised to find that they had unintentionally reproduced the classic lesions of Alexander disease.
"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy – the GFAP protein," says Messing.

Having originally looked at existing FDA-approved drugs to see if any could have an impact on Alexander disease, the researchers eventually decided to design their own, custom drug to reduce GFAP production levels.
The drug works through antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small bits of DNA that suppress GFAP production. The treatment was tested in animals before a clinical trial in humans began in 2021.

An injection into the spinal canal once every three months, delivered by a healthcare professional, is required to administer Zanvastro. The approval covers patients of all ages, though signs of the disease most commonly appear before age 2.

As one mother of a child with Alexander disease puts it, describing her daughter's response to treatment: "The fog's being lifted on her brain, and her personality gets a chance to come out more and more."

It's still not a cure – it doesn't reverse the condition or make it disappear – but it can significantly slow the progression of the disease and improve symptoms by targeting the underlying causes directly.
"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," says Messing.

articles.title: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived

paras.en: A 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals a lost world where early humans lived
- Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee

- A remarkably preserved elephant tooth dating back nearly 700,000 years has revealed a surprisingly lush prehistoric world where giant elephants and early humans lived side by side. Discovered in northern Israel alongside ancient stone tools, the tooth belonged to a straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Ice Age.

A single ancient elephant tooth is offering scientists a remarkable glimpse into a world that existed nearly 700,000 years ago. Found in northern Israel, the fossil has helped researchers reconstruct a surprisingly lush prehistoric landscape filled with forests, rivers, wetlands, and abundant vegetation. This ancient environment supported enormous elephants and some of the region's earliest human populations, revealing how access to water and natural resources may have helped our ancestors survive and move between continents.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The discovery comes from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (GBY-NBA), an archaeological site where early humans produced stone tools hundreds of thousands of years ago. Elephant remains were unearthed alongside handaxes and cleavers made from basalt, a volcanic rock. These implements belong to the Acheulian tradition, one of the oldest and most widespread stone tool technologies in human history.

The research, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, was led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University). The team examined a large elephant molar and fragments of tusk recovered from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), situated in the Jordan Rift Valley just south of today's Hula Valley. The site was excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues.
A Giant Elephant Tooth Reveals a Lost Prehistoric World

The fossils belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, commonly known as the straight-tusked elephant. This enormous prehistoric animal was among the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene, the geological period that included the most recent ice ages.

Rather than focusing only on the animal itself, the scientists treated its tooth as a record of the world in which it lived. Teeth can preserve chemical clues about an animal's diet and surroundings, allowing researchers to investigate environmental conditions from hundreds of thousands of years ago.

To uncover those clues, the team combined several scientific techniques, including CT scans, 3D reconstruction, microscopic examination of tooth wear, isotope geochemistry, and pollen analysis. CT imaging allowed them to examine the fossil's internal structure, while chemical measurements and microscopic evidence helped build a picture of the ancient habitat.

The results pointed to a remarkably persistent landscape containing woodlands, open grasslands, marshes, flowing rivers, and shallow bodies of water. Carbon isotope measurements suggested that the elephant lived in an environment with a dependable water supply. Meanwhile, pollen preserved in nearby sediments revealed a variety of wetland plants, including reeds, sedges, willow, tamarisk, and aquatic vegetation.
Together, these findings suggest that the region offered a diverse and productive environment capable of supporting both giant mammals and early human communities.
An Ancient Oasis Along a Crucial Human Migration Route

The location of this prehistoric landscape makes the discovery particularly significant. The Hula Valley lies within the Levantine Corridor, a natural passage connecting Africa and Eurasia that played an important role in the movements of ancient humans and animals.

Researchers believe the area functioned as a relatively stable ecological refuge, maintaining vital habitats and resources over long periods. Its rivers, wetlands, forests, and grasslands would have offered dependable sources of water, vegetation, and animal life for populations traveling through the region.

For early humans, access to such environments could have made the difference between surviving in an unfamiliar landscape and being unable to sustain a population. Understanding these habitats may therefore help explain how ancient human groups moved through the region and adapted to changing environmental conditions.
According to Prof. Sharon, "understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species."

The findings highlight the importance of studying ancient landscapes alongside the fossils and artifacts found within them. By reconstructing the environments that supported prehistoric life, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the conditions that influenced early human survival and migration.

"The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive," Sharon says. "The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world's earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago."

The study brought together specialists from several Israeli universities. Farrell of the University of Haifa conducted the research using material from the site excavated by Sharon and his colleagues. Additional collaborators included Cheryl A. Makarewicz (isotope studies) and Nimrod Marom (archaeozoology) of the University of Haifa, as well as Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut (pollen studies) of Tel Aviv University.

articles.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

paras.en: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

- A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.

A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.

Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.

"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.

Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.
Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years

To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.

At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.

Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.

Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.

Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.

Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.
High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline
The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.

After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.
That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.

Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.
Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes
When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.

Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.

The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.
Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.
Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.

Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.
Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?
The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.

"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."

Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.

In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.

The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.
The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

articles.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms

paras.en: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms

- Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.

Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.

The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.
A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms

To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.

Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.

The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.

These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.
A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality

"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.

The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.

The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).

"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."
Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?

Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.
Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.

"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.

However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.
"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.

If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.

articles.title: The universe in the eye of a telescope | Space photo of the day for Oct. 29, 2026
articles.author: Anthony Wood

paras.en: Stars shine in the vast aluminum dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) in this photograph captured by astronomer and astrophotographer José Rodrigues during a recent visit to the European Southern Observatory's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

Rodrigues' image captures "airglow" infusing the night sky over La Silla with a soft orange glow, which is created as sunlight interacts with molecules in the upper atmosphere, according to the University of Lancaster.

The subtle phenomenon can be seen reflected in the 15-meter (49-foot) primary dish of the SEST telescope along with the myriad stars of the Southern Hemisphere, as the dome of the ESO's 3.6-meter telescope looms in the background.

"Despite knowing about its 15-meter diameter beforehand, I was amazed by its size," Rodrigues noted in the ESO image release. The SEST first opened its great eye to the universe in 1987, at which time it was the only large telescope in the Southern Hemisphere tasked with collecting submillimeter wavelengths of light that exist beyond the visible light spectrum.

These specific wavelengths of light are emitted by wandering comets and colossal clouds of cold molecular dust and gas threaded throughout the Milky Way and beyond. SEST's observations improved our knowledge of ancient galaxies, star formation and so much more, with its perch 2,375 meters (7,792 feet) above sea level granting it a near unrivalled view of the heavens above.
The SEST telescope was decommissioned in 2003, though its work was continued by the more capable Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA).

With its working days over, the SEST telescope now stands as a quiet mirror reflecting the stars of the Southern Hemisphere night sky, seemingly pondering mysteries of the universe that it once tried to solve

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.
